Response: Hospitals were assured that their acquisition cost data would remain confidential as part of the ODACS data collection and analysis process, and this protection will be honored. Publishing de-identified survey data with anonymized hospital characteristics appended still presents an immense confidentiality risk due to the small number of respondent hospitals identified in multiple specific categories ( e.g., rural hospitals in specific Census regions). For details on methodology and results, CMS refers commenters to the ODACS Technical Report. Further, CMS has provided additional detail on methods and analysis results in comment response throughout this final rule with comment period.
C. CY 2027 OPPS Payment Methodology for 340B Purchased Drugs Based on Survey Results
As described previously, section 1833(t)(14)(D)(ii) of the Act requires the Secretary to conduct periodic surveys to determine the hospital acquisition cost for each SCOD for use in setting the payment rates for SCODs under section 1833(t)(14)(A) of the Act. Section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act provides that the payment amount for a SCOD for a year is equal to the average acquisition cost for the drug (which at the option of the Secretary, may vary by hospital group) as determined by the Secretary, taking into account the survey data collected under subparagraph (D) of section 1833(t)(14) of the Act. Based on our analysis of the survey data, the most immediately evident and significant difference found between Medicare payment and acquisition cost was for 340B drugs acquired by 340B-participating hospitals, where the selected methodology shows that aggregate acquisition costs were approximately ASP minus 33.4 percent. This indicates average acquisition costs that were 37.2 percent lower than the general OPPS payment rate (ASP plus six percent). These results clearly demonstrate that ASP plus 6 percent is not an appropriate payment proxy for hospitals that acquire drugs through the 340B Program. Consequently, we proposed to adjust the OPPS payment policy for 340B drugs to better align payment with the acquisition costs demonstrated by the survey. Specifically, for CY 2027, we proposed to pay for drugs acquired under the 340B Program at ASP minus 33.4 percent.
Conversely, for non-340B drugs, after taking into account the survey data, we proposed to maintain the current payment rate, which is generally ASP plus 6 percent, under the authority at section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act. As displayed in Table 67, the heterogeneity in acquisition costs for non-340B drugs is slightly greater than for 340B drugs; this variation has led us to believe this area warrants additional analysis by CMS and input from interested parties. The results of the survey for non-340B drugs generally indicate lower acquisition costs than current OPPS payment; however, the ( printed page 70527) discrepancy is not as clear and significant as with 340B drugs. Therefore, we are continuing to analyze the data from this survey, aligning those reported costs with hospital claims billing patterns, to see if any additional significant trends exist that merit further adjustments to OPPS payment policy in future years. We are also assessing billing patterns among those hospitals that did not respond. Finally, we collected and analyzed information on non-NDC-specific GPO discounts that hospitals receive and are still considering how these discounts could be factored into future analysis and policymaking. We will consider these issues for future rulemaking.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Many commenters supported our proposal to pay for 340B-acquired drugs at ASP minus 33.4 percent based on the survey results. These commenters stated that aligning the 340B payment rate more closely with hospitals' actual acquisition costs, as reflected by the survey data, would improve the accuracy of Medicare payment, reduce incentives to choose more expensive drugs or shift drug administration to higher-cost settings, promote transparency and accountability, direct statutorily-required budget-neutral savings toward non-drug OPPS services and help ensure beneficiaries share in the value of 340B discounts through lower cost sharing. A commenter stated that CMS's findings are consistent with analyses from the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC) and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS OIG) showing that Medicare payments for 340B-acquired drugs have substantially exceeded 340B drug acquisition costs. A commenter endorsed the proposal on the basis that it is a reasonable and overdue correction to the way Medicare pays hospitals for administering drugs. Another commenter stated that this policy reflects that Federal payment rates should rest on evidence of what something actually costs. A commenter stated that the survey made evident that the acquisition cost for SCODs through the 340B Program is far lower than the statutory default rate of ASP plus six percent and that with this clear survey data, CMS is required to set payment based on the average acquisition cost for 340B-acquired drugs. Citing our example of a beneficiary's coinsurance alone exceeding the entire price the hospital paid for the drug, many commenters emphasized the positive effect the proposed policy would have in reducing beneficiary drug copayments due to those copayments being calculated based on the amount Medicare pays the hospital rather than the hospital's acquisition cost for the drug.
Response: We thank commenters for their support.
Comments: Many of these commenters additionally provided criticisms of the 340B Program generally and proposed various reforms for CMS to consider to address those criticisms.
Response: We note feedback related to 340B Program policies are outside the scope of the proposed rule and are not addressed in this final rule with comment period. However, we thank the commenters for their insights and concerns.
Comment: A few commenters commented on our observation in the proposed rule (91 FR 41880) that we received a number of letters in response to the survey, many of which appeared to be coordinated form letters, from eligible hospitals indicating that they would not be providing their acquisition data and explaining their reasons for not doing so. A commenter stated that they supported our proposed payment policy, despite what the commenter believes was a concerted effort to obstruct the survey. Another commenter challenged our observation that we received a number of responses, many of which appeared to be coordinated form letters, from eligible hospitals indicating that they would not be providing their acquisition data and explaining their reasons for not doing so. The commenter stated that there is no proof of coordinated non-response among 340B-participating hospitals.
Response: We disagree that there is no proof of a coordinated response. The hundreds of nearly identical letters and email templates themselves supply evidence of such coordination. We find it highly unlikely that hundreds of hospitals would independently submit letters informing us that they would not be providing their acquisition cost data and explaining their alleged reasons for not doing so using identical or nearly identical language. The record also reflects that several large law firms publicly promoted such a strategy.[128]
Additionally, shortly after the survey first launched, several major hospital associations purporting to represent more than 3,000 hospitals paid under OPPS jointly issued a widely publicized letter to CMS claiming that it was wrong of CMS to tell hospitals they “are to” respond to the survey.[129] CMS made this requirement clear by publishing in numerous places throughout the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC proposed and final rule, the OMB-approved PRA package, and educational materials that the survey was required of hospitals. These hospital associations made no known attempt to help their member hospitals complete the survey and fulfil their statutory obligation; rather, the record reflects that these hospital associations cast doubt on the requirement for survey participation and encouraged non-compliance among their member hospitals. These same hospital associations now criticize the response rate to the survey, incorrectly claiming that not enough hospitals responded for ( printed page 70528) CMS to make the necessary, statutory payment determinations.
Comment: Many commenters stated that the payment reductions would threaten their ability to continue providing services, particularly to low-income, uninsured, under-insured, geographically isolated, medically complex and other vulnerable patients. Many commenters stated that the effect of the payment reductions and corresponding budget neutrality increase would be to subsidize for-profit hospitals at the expense of 340B hospitals and the vulnerable populations they serve.
Response: We are not persuaded that more closely aligning our payment amounts for 340B-acquired drugs with their acquisition costs would threaten 340B hospitals' ability to continue to provide services to vulnerable patients or would constitute a subsidization of for-profit hospitals at the expense of 340B hospitals and those patients. Although 340B hospitals would receive reduced payment for 340B drugs, they would also receive the same percentage increase to payments for non-drug items and services as non-340B hospitals. Further, this policy ensures that the reduced drug costs, and associated reduced drug cost sharing obligations, are passed directly to the beneficiaries that these hospitals serve. We acknowledge that some hospitals will potentially experience greater reductions to drug payments than increases to non-drug items and services as a consequence of our policy. However, that does not change our statutory obligation under section 1833(t)(14) of the Act to conduct a survey of drug acquisition costs and adjust payment rates taking those costs into account.
Comment: Many commenters stated that the proposed reduction was contrary to the Congressional intent behind the 340B program, which was designed to enable covered entities to stretch scarce Federal resources as far as possible to provide services to low-income and uninsured patients. Many commenters also stated that CMS had failed to account for the effect of the proposal on 340B hospitals and that failure renders the proposed policy arbitrary and capricious.
Response: We disagree that we have failed to account for the effect of the proposal in formulating and proposing our policy, and we do not agree with commenters that our proposed policy is contrary to the Congressional intent behind the 340B program. We are fulfilling our statutory obligation under section 1833(t)(14) of the Act to periodically conduct a survey of hospital acquisition costs and use the resulting data to inform payment rates. The purpose of the proposed policy is to better align our payment amounts for 340B-acquired drugs with their actual acquisition costs as demonstrated by the survey.
Comment: Many commenters expressed concern about the combined economic effect of the 340B drug payment proposal, the remedy proposal and the expansion of the volume control method. Many of these commenters cited the millions of dollars they expected to lose as a result of these policies. These commenters urged CMS not to view these proposals in isolation but to evaluate their cumulative effect. Many of these commenters additionally referenced “severe financial headwinds” that they are experiencing due to a variety of past and impending economic factors.
Response: We recognize that the cumulative economic effect of the policies we are proposing for CY 2027, along with the financial circumstances hospitals have faced over the past few years, may be significant for some hospitals. However, we believe these effects must be balanced against the windfalls hospitals received previously that we are statutorily obligated and/or have the discretion to recover, our obligations under section 1833(t)(14) of the Act to periodically conduct surveys of hospitals' drug acquisition costs and take that data into account in setting payment rates, and our responsibility to adopt methods to control unnecessary increases in the volume of covered OPD services.
Comment: Many commenters urged us to delay or phase-in (or both) the implementation of the proposal. Commenters suggested that delaying implementation would provide additional time for CMS to conduct a more complete hospital-level impact analysis of the combined effect of the 340B drug payment proposal, the remedy proposal and the site neutral proposal and other OPPS payment changes. Another commenter suggested that CMS could use the delay to establish a limit on how much money hospitals could lose if they rely heavily on 340B drugs and develop a methodology that would ensure a more equitable distribution of the savings resulting from the proposed payment reduction. Commenters also noted that an implementation delay would provide interested parties with additional time to comment on the payment proposal and underlying survey. Commenters that recommended phasing-in the payment policy recommended that we do so over multiple years and stated that it would allow hospitals and CMS to evaluate the actual effects on access, service availability, beneficiary cost sharing, and hospital financial stability before the full reduction takes effect. Commenters also stated that it would give hospitals time to adapt to the financial impact of the policy and help avoid abrupt disruptions to patient services.
Response: We understand commenters' emphasis on taking a measured approach to implementing the proposal. However, we believe that the payment misalignment that our proposed policy will address has been in effect for many years and it is important to implement this policy now that we have conducted the required survey and have data clearly demonstrating that the existing payment rate for 340B-acquired drugs is not even close to a representative proxy for the cost of their acquisition. Given the extent of the payment misalignment identified by the survey results and the length of time the misalignment has likely been in place, we think that delaying or phasing-in the changes would be inconsistent with our obligations under section 1833(t)(14) of the Act and our goal of ensuring that Medicare and Medicare beneficiaries are paying for drugs commensurate with the cost of their acquisition.
Comment: Many commenters opposed the proposal on the grounds that it would establish a dangerous precedent that non-Medicare payers might follow. These commenters stressed that Medicare payment policies often influence other entities, such as Medicaid or commercial payers, to “piggyback” off CMS' payment decisions. These commenters expressed concern that this would fundamentally undermine the purpose and effectiveness of the 340B program to financially assist hospitals that serve a high volume of low-income patients.
Response: We do not have control over how our proposed policy might influence other non-CMS payers in the future. What those other payers may or may not do in the future would not be a valid reason for us to refrain from better aligning OPPS payment for 340B-acquired drugs with their acquisition costs as demonstrated by the survey, consistent with section 1833(t)(14)(iii)(I) of the Act.
Comment: Several commenters expressed concern about the indirect implications of the proposal to pay ASP minus 33.4 percent for 340B-acquired drugs for providers that contract with Medicare Advantage (MA) organizations. Commenters stated that MA organizations and private PBMs ( printed page 70529) will cite these OPPS rate reductions as justification to impose their own cuts for 340B drugs, further weakening the ability to utilize 340B savings. Commenters urged CMS to clarify that the proposed payment methodology of ASP minus 33.4 percent, including any downstream budget neutral impacts, is Original Medicare (OM) payment policy and does not itself establish, require or permit a corresponding payment reduction under MA contracts.
Response: We appreciate feedback on this issue. CMS establishes payment policies and payment rates for services payable under OM through a separate, distinct process that is not directly related to terms of private contracting arrangements between MA organizations and providers. Further, section 1854(a)(6)(B)(iii) of the Act prohibits CMS from requiring an MA organization to contract with a particular hospital, physician, or other entity to furnish items and services, including 340B-acquired drugs, or requiring a particular price structure for payment under such a contract. Providers and MA organizations may engage in dispute resolution under existing contracts and any contract negotiations or re-negotiations independently of CMS. MAOs must pay non-contract providers or facilities for services and items at least the amount they would have received under OM payment rules, in accordance with section 1852(a)(2) of the Act.
1. Statistically Significant Estimate
Under section 1833(t)(14)(D)(iii) of the Act, the periodic surveys conducted by the Secretary under section 1833(t)(14)(D)(ii) of the Act must “have a large sample of hospitals that is sufficient to generate a statistically significant estimate of the average hospital acquisition cost for each specified covered outpatient drug.” Our survey results meet this standard, particularly because hospital acquisition cost is a price measure.[130] Reliable price measures require far less sampling than quantity or revenue measures because markets tend to compress this distribution of prices across transactions but do not compress the distribution of quantities or expenditures.[131] While hospital acquisition cost for a branded drug would not be exactly equal across hospitals in the 340B Program, it would not differ by a factor of 1000 and rarely even a factor of 2. Because the standard errors of the 340B-hospital sample mean and the non-340B-hospital sample mean are each proportional to the standard deviation of the underlying population, a compressed price distribution translates directly into small standard errors and high statistical significance.[132]
As discussed previously and shown in Table 74, the 95 percent confidence intervals for 340B drugs were relatively narrow, ranging from approximately 34.7 percent to 32.3 percent below ASP for the unadjusted margin and from approximately 34.3 percent to 32.1 percent below ASP for the IPW-adjusted margin. These results support the statistical validity of the estimated acquisition cost margins and indicate that the survey data provide reliable estimates of the acquisition cost discounts realized by 340B hospitals relative to ASP. These sampling requirements for price measurement are well known in national accounting. For example, the Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics measures prices for the Consumer Price Index (CPI) using about 100,000 commodity-and-service price observations per month, while the Producer Price Index (PPI) uses approximately 64,000 monthly price quotations from about 16,000 establishments.[133] These samples are tiny relative to the transactions they are designed to represent: the CPI commodity-and-service sample alone is less than 0.01 percent of such payments.[134]
In our efforts to obtain data from a statistically significant sample of hospitals paid under the OPPS, we initially included for survey participation 100 percent of OPPS hospitals. From this, we received replies from 53.3 percent of non-340B hospitals and 28.6 percent of 340B hospitals. These response rates are similar to past surveys of health care providers as determined by a separate meta-analysis [135] and have resulted in sample sizes that show significant differences in acquisition costs between the two hospital categories.[136] While we applied data cleaning to exclude specific survey records with anomalous or implausible data, very few hospitals were excluded from our population: only 27 subunits that reported identical and duplicative data to their parent unit. Additionally, while we applied refinements to narrow the population of hospitals to only those who either responded to the survey or had OPPS claims for survey-relevant HCPCS codes, these refinements did not remove any hospital with relevant data from analysis. These efforts were undertaken to maintain the largest possible pool of hospitals and data to evaluate. It is our view based on efforts to sensitivity test the responses and reweight the findings that the conclusion of statistical difference in the average acquisition costs for 340B and non-340B hospitals would likely not change.
Comment: Multiple commenters concurred with CMS that the survey generated a statistically significant estimate. One commenter stated that:
CMS opened the survey to all hospitals that received OPPS payments for outpatient drugs during the survey period. Because this survey was meant to determine hospital acquisition costs for outpatient drugs paid under OPPS, this is the correct universe. As explained in the survey, 3,147 entities were eligible to complete it. Of these, 1,343 (42.7%) submitted a response and 1,304 reported acquisitions of one of the surveyed drugs. While the statutory text “a large sample” has no objective meaning, nor does it have any statistical definition, expert judgment is called for to determine whether the CMS survey's sample would qualify. There are several ( printed page 70530) reasons to believe it does. For one, this sample is larger than the original GAO survey conducted in 2005. In that survey, the original, official survey conducted as required by statute, only 1,157 hospitals responded. GAO determined that this sample was “reliable for estimating [Specified Covered Outpatient Drugs] prices.” It went on to say that estimates of prices were more precise for drugs purchased by many hospitals. Further, the responding hospitals included hospitals across the relevant categories defined by GAO and frequently used in health care policy, such as teaching and non-teaching, urban and rural. Because each category was represented in the final sample, there was data CMS was able to use to transform the results such that they would match the population of hospitals, similar to how political polls feature weights such that they can reflect an entire voting population.
CMS employed a census-based approach that sought information from all hospitals relevant to the proposed policy and ultimately obtained responses from a substantial number of hospitals, generating what [the commenter] understands to be the largest volume of acquisition cost data for hospital outpatient drugs ever collected in connection with the Medicare program. After applying appropriate data-cleaning and validation procedures, CMS used inverse probability weighting to account for differential response rates among hospital types and evaluated the resulting estimates using established statistical techniques. Importantly, the survey produced a narrow 95 percent confidence interval for the acquisition cost of 340B-acquired drugs, with estimates ranging only from ASP minus 32.3 percent to ASP minus 34.7 percent (a range of only 2.4 percentage points). CMS calculated these confidence intervals using 10,000 bootstrap replications, a sound and established statistical technique designed to assess the precision and reliability of survey estimates. The narrowness of this confidence interval confirms that the survey data are reliable and sufficiently precise for purposes of informing CMS's determination of the average acquisition cost of 340B-acquired drugs and implementing an acquisition-cost-based payment methodology. Moreover, CMS's approach to addressing nonrespondents likely results in a more conservative estimate of the discount associated with 340B-acquired drugs and therefore is favorable to 340B hospitals. CMS used inverse probability weighting to ensure that responding hospitals appropriately represented nonresponding hospitals in the overall population, a methodology that is widely accepted and that improved the representativeness of the final sample. To the extent that 340B hospitals with the lowest acquisition costs were less likely to respond, CMS's weighting methodology would tend to increase estimated acquisition costs for 340B-discounted drugs relative to the acquisition costs that might have been observed had all hospitals responded. Thus, if anything, the survey methodology is more likely to overstate average acquisition costs for 340B-acquired drugs than understate them. Taken together, the survey's large volume of data, rigorous weighting methodology, and narrow confidence intervals provide strong support for CMS's conclusion that the survey generated a statistically significant and reliable estimate of the average acquisition cost of 340B-acquired drugs.
Finally, a third commenter found the survey to be
[. . .]methodologically sound and has response rates that compare favorably to other drug cost surveys, such as the National Average Drug Acquisition Cost (NADAC) survey, which CMS has relied on for over a decade as the accepted benchmark for Medicaid fee-for-service pharmacy reimbursement. The ODACS identified 4,494 survey-eligible hospitals and all valid survey responses were used in the analysis. Of the initial population, 43.6 percent of hospitals submitted a response. This design and response profile appears robust when compared to NADAC. NADAC similarly collects voluntary, invoice-level net acquisition cost data from a random monthly sample of independent and chain retail community pharmacies but only 18-24 percent of surveyed pharmacies respond to the monthly survey request, a response rate below the 41.4 to 43.6 percent range achieved by the ODACS. The ODACS's methodology and point estimates provide compelling evidence for reducing 340B drug payment rates under OPPS.
Response: We thank commenters for their support. We concur with their assessment that our survey meets and exceeds the statutory standard.
Comment: Many commenters contended that CMS did not meet statutorily specified requirements to “conduct a survey . . . to determine the hospital acquisition cost for each specified covered outpatient drug” and raised concerns that the survey did not “have a large sample of hospitals that is sufficient to generate a statistically significant estimate of the average hospital acquisition cost for each specified covered outpatient drug.” Commenters pointed to the fact that drugs for which fewer than 10 survey responses were received were dropped from the final margin calculations as evidence that CMS did not demonstrate that the survey sample was large enough to support statistically significant estimates of the average acquisition cost for each, individual outpatient drug.
Response: We disagree with the statement that the survey lacked adequate breadth and achieved an insufficient response rate to analyze the universe of specified covered outpatient drugs in a statistically significant manner. To the contrary, CMS fulfilled its statutory duties to request, collect, and analyze data for each specified covered outpatient drug. CMS gave nearly 4,500 hospitals the opportunity to submit their acquisition cost data for consideration. The survey included 1,843 NDCs for outpatient drugs and biological products, corresponding to 519 HCPCS codes. All but 10 drugs with nonzero outpatient claims utilization received at least one survey response. The drugs that received at least one survey response represent virtually all Medicare use and spending, comprising 99.9 percent of payment for survey-relevant outpatient drugs from July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025. The fact that some low-volume drugs received fewer responses—consistent with their utilization patterns in practice—does not invalidate the data collected by the survey instrument or make it inapplicable for policymaking.
Commenters referenced the fact that outlier identification required the exclusion of drugs with fewer than 10 hospitals reporting acquisitions. While CMS excluded drugs that received fewer than 10 survey responses in the process of outlier identification, this enabled us to retain the vast majority of HCPCS codes during this stage of analysis, particularly in the context of overall use and spending. Even with this restriction applied, we retained observations for drugs representing 93.8 percent of Medicare payment for survey-relevant outpatient drugs from July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025. CMS also reiterates that outlier identification and trimming is only one aspect of the survey analysis process, and extensive analyses were performed upon the full population of data received.
Section 1833(t)(14)(D)(iii) of the Act requires that the survey have a “large sample of hospitals that is sufficient to generate a statistically significant estimate of the average hospital acquisition cost for each specified covered outpatient drug” but does not ( printed page 70531) specify how this is to be determined. While GAO deemed a response rate of 1,000 out of 3,450 eligible hospitals would meet the requirement for a large sample when designing the initial surveys in 2004 and 2005, their assessment—specific to their survey design and constraints at the time—does not constitute a specific, authoritative response rate that all subsequent surveys must precisely meet. We reiterate that our survey design invited 100 percent of the 4,494 eligible hospitals to participate, and approximately 41 percent of the refined population of 3,147 hospitals reported acquiring surveyed drugs. Additionally, the volume of data collected overall through ODACS is substantially larger than what was collected in GAO's initial surveys: GAO only considered 53 non-radiopharmaceutical outpatient drug HCPCS codes in their surveys of hospitals' reported acquisition costs, a tenth of the number of Part B drug HCPCS codes that were analyzed through ODACS. As such, our survey greatly exceeds the comprehensiveness of GAO's survey in terms of included hospitals and drugs. Furthermore, as detailed in section V.B.8.b of this final rule, the data received in the CMS survey produced statistically significant results—particularly for 340B-acquired drugs—that are representative of the overall survey-eligible population as shown through the IPW and confidence interval analyses among other factors cited in this final rule. Detailed discussion of the statistical significance of the data collected through ODACS can be found in the ODACS Technical Report and elsewhere in this final rule.
2. Grouping Hospitals by 340B Covered Entity Status
Section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to set the amount of payment for SCODs at an amount equal “to the average acquisition cost for the drug for that year (which, at the option of the Secretary, may vary by hospital group (as defined by the Secretary based on volume of covered OPD services or other relevant characteristics)), as determined by the Secretary taking into account the hospital acquisition cost survey data under subparagraph (D).”
In accordance with this authority, we proposed to vary the amount of payment for 340B-acquired drugs by the group of hospitals that are enrolled in the 340B Program as 340B covered entity hospitals because their drug acquisition costs vary significantly from those not enrolled in that program. The significant drug acquisition cost discounts that 340B covered entity hospitals receive for 340B-acquired drugs enable these hospitals to acquire drugs at much lower costs than non-340B hospitals incur for the same drugs. Accordingly, we proposed to use 340B covered entity status as a relevant characteristic to group hospitals for purposes of payment based on average acquisition cost under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act. Therefore, for 340B drugs acquired by 340B covered entity hospitals, we proposed changes to better align Medicare payment with average acquisition cost for the drug as specified in statute.
As discussed in more detail below, for drugs not acquired through the 340B Program, we proposed that 340B and non-340B hospitals would continue to receive payment at a payment rate that is generally ASP plus 6 percent.
We acknowledged (91 FR 41888) we could set a single payment rate for a drug for a hospital group (such as 340B hospitals) regardless of whether the drug was acquired through the 340B Program, but that does not align with our intent to more appropriately align payment with acquisition costs. As such, we are only applying the reduced payment rate to drugs acquired through the 340B Program by the hospital group defined as 340B hospitals, as this most appropriately aligns payment with acquisition cost of drugs of this hospital group. For non-340B drugs acquired by 340B hospitals, we proposed that payment will not be adjusted. We sought comment on these proposals. Specifically, we sought comment on our proposal to use 340B covered entity status as a relevant characteristic to group hospitals for purposes of payment based on average acquisition cost under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act and our proposal to vary the amount of payment for 340B-acquired drugs by the group of hospitals that are enrolled in the 340B Program to more appropriately align payment with the average acquisition cost for the drug.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Many commenters supported our proposal to vary the amount of payment for 340B-acquired drugs by the group of hospitals that are enrolled in the 340B Program. These commenters stated that doing so would better align payment for these drugs with their acquisition cost, resulting in more accurate Medicare payment and reduced beneficiary copayment for these drugs.
Response: We thank the commenters for their support.
Comment: Many commenters stated that CMS lacks the authority under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act to vary payments by groups defined by 340B Program participation. These commenters characterized CMS' proposal to do so as arbitrary and capricious, contrary to the text of the Medicare statute, and not in accordance with 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A). These commenters recognized the Secretary's authority under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) to vary payment “by hospital group (as defined by the Secretary based on volume of covered OPD services or other relevant characteristics)” but stated that 340B status is not a relevant characteristic. They stated that 340B status is not a relevant characteristic because 340B Program participation designations are not CMS hospital groups, but rather determinations made by a separate agency unrelated to Medicare program considerations. They stated that the intent of Congress was never to include participation in the 340B Program, a Federal program codified in another statute, the Public Health Service Act, as a characteristic that should be used to vary payment. One of these commenters stated that:
If Congress intended 340B participation to be used as a factor to differentiate Medicare drug payment, it would have included it as one of the relevant characteristics in establishing the SCOD payment rate methodology, given that in passing the [Medicare Modernization Act] in 2003, the 340B program had already been in existence for over a decade. That is, Congress well knew that 340B hospitals had lower acquisition costs. Congress chose not to reference 340B in its SCOD reimbursement methodology but also took additional steps to ensure 340B prices do not affect Medicare reimbursement. It would be counterintuitive for Congress to enact a program that is intended to enable hospitals to purchase certain drugs at lower acquisition costs and realize savings through these discounts, only to completely eliminate the benefit of these discounts on Medicare drugs—a sizable portion of 340B hospitals' utilization—by allowing CMS to set their payment rate at 340B acquisition cost. In passing the 340B statute, Congress intended that the 340B program would function by allowing covered entities to purchase these drugs at lower costs and to retain the difference between reimbursement and the drug purchase price as a way to allow them to `stretch scarce Federal resources as far as possible, reaching ( printed page 70532) more eligible patients and providing more comprehensive services.'
In support of their argument, the commenter pointed to the absence of 340B status on CMS enrollment forms, GAO reports from 2004 and 2005 in which the GAO did not include 340B participation as a relevant characteristic when examining differences in hospital acquisition costs, and Congress's exclusion of 340B prices from the calculation of ASP under section 1847A(c)(2)(A) of the Act.
Response: We do not agree that we lack the authority under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act to vary payments by groups defined by 340B Program participation. Section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to establish appropriate Medicare OPPS payment rates for covered outpatient drugs equal to the average acquisition cost for the drug for that year (which, at the option of the Secretary, may vary by hospital group (as defined by the Secretary based on volume of covered OPD services or other relevant characteristics)), as determined by the Secretary taking into account the hospital acquisition cost survey data under subparagraph (D). As demonstrated by its plain language, the best reading of the statute is that it delegates significant discretionary authority to the Secretary. We do not see anything in the statute that would limit the Secretary's discretion in the manner described by commenters. The Secretary is generally empowered to define hospital groups “based on volume of covered OPD services or other relevant characteristics” and there is nothing in section 1833(t)(14) of the Act or elsewhere to indicate the Secretary is foreclosed from defining a hospital group based on a hospital's voluntary participation in a program (the 340B Program) that has a direct and significant effect on the hospital's ability to acquire drugs at a substantial discount.
As described earlier in this section, we assessed a variety of hospital characteristics, such as hospital size, 340B participation status, ODACS drug purchase volume, outpatient drug claims billing volume, rurality, geographic location, GPO membership, GPO discount amount, and teaching status. Our detailed analysis found that 340B drug acquisition resulted in a nearly 40 percent differential from current Medicare payment, by far the most significant discrepancy between current Medicare payment and hospital acquisition cost, clearly making 340B status a relevant characteristic[ ] for purposes of varying OPPS payment.
After consideration of public comments we are finalizing our proposal to vary the amount of payment for 340B-acquired drugs by the group of hospitals that are enrolled in the 340B Program as 340B covered entity hospitals.
3. Applying a Single Reduction Percentage to ASP for 340B-Acquired Drugs
Section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act provides that the payment amount for a SCOD for a year is equal to the average acquisition cost for the drug “as determined by the Secretary taking into account” the survey data collected under subparagraph (D). In accordance with this authority, we proposed to apply a single discount factor to ASP for drugs acquired by 340B hospitals in lieu of calculating individual acquisition cost amounts for 340B-acquired drugs. Applying a single discount factor to ASP creates a standardized payment reduction. Conversely, calculating individual acquisition costs links reimbursement directly to the exact, variable purchase prices hospitals pay for specific 340B drugs.
We considered calculating payment rates derived from individual acquisition cost amounts for 340B drugs; however, given the dynamic nature of drug pricing we concluded that it would be more appropriate to apply a single discount factor to ASP. We believe this is more appropriate as ASP is also dynamic in nature. ASP changes over time (quarter to quarter), so tying the payment amount to an average discount of ASP results in a more accurate payment amount, by quarter, than if hospitals had to wait until the next survey cycle.
Each drug HCPCS code has its own specific payment rate calculated that is unique to the drug described by the applicable HCPCS code. We would apply an average discount, calculated as described previously under V.B.9.b. and V.B.9.c.(2). of this final rule with comment period, to the drug-specific ASP amount. This makes our proposed payment rate specific to the average acquisition cost for the drug. Applying the payment rate in this manner also allows for this average discount to apply to newly calculated ASPs as they are updated on a quarterly basis. It would not be practical to calculate a drug-specific payment rate for each NDC, and each HCPCS code, based on the survey data, as the survey-collected data is based on a snapshot in time and would not reflect future changes in average acquisition costs. Therefore, as drug prices change, we believe it is appropriate and reasonable to continue to update the calculated ASPs and then to reduce payments by an appropriate percentage of ASP to better align payment with the average cost of the drug.
As an alternative to establishing one aggregate discount amount based on survey data, we considered establishing one aggregate discount amount based on 340B ceiling prices from HRSA.[137] Under this alternative, we would use HRSA's 340B ceiling price data, rather than survey data, to calculate an average discount. As described previously, when assessing the 340B ceiling price, we calculated an analogous acquisition cost margin of ASP minus 28 percent for 340B drugs, which was calculated as the difference between the 340B ceiling price for each NDC in the survey and ASPs that were volume-weighted by 340B OPPS claims data utilization during the duration of the survey. We believed this could be a reasonable alternative to our proposal, as it is based on objective data, can be updated regularly (such as quarterly or annually) with the release of new ceiling prices and new claims utilization data, and significantly diminishes the discrepancy between Medicare payment and hospital acquisition costs for these drugs. We sought comment on this alternative to set OPPS payment for 340B acquired drugs at ASP minus 28.0 percent, per the methodology described to calculate this OPPS claims volume weighted mean margin of the 340B ceiling price from ASP. We note this figure is volume-weighted using OPPS claims data for the duration of the survey, but we also solicited comment on volume-weighting this average based on the claims data available for the applicable calendar year in which the policy would be effective. For example, for the CY 2027 rule, this would be volume-weighted based on claims data available for that year's rule, which would be claims data from CY 2025. At the end of this section in the proposed rule, we also provide estimated impacts of this alternative policy proposal of ASP minus 28 percent based on the 340B ceiling price data, so interested parties were aware of these impacts if CMS ( printed page 70533) ultimately adopted this policy for CY 2027.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Multiple commenters supported our proposal to apply a uniform ASP adjustment rather than a drug-specific adjustment. A commenter stated that “to the extent CMS's proposed reimbursement rate accurately reflects surveyed acquisition costs, [the commenter] supports the proposed rate, whether CMS ultimately finalizes ASP minus 33.4 percent or another rate supported by the data, such as ASP minus 28 percent as discussed in the proposed rule. The proposal will reduce Medicare and beneficiary spending that exceeds hospitals' acquisition costs, advancing both program integrity and beneficiary affordability.” Another commenter agreed with CMS that the proposed payment rate for 340B-acquired drugs “more accurately reflects the hospital acquisition cost, and we respectfully urge CMS to finalize this proposed payment change.”
Response: We thank commenters for their support.
Comment: Many commenters opposed CMS's proposal to apply a uniform ASP adjustment rather than a drug-specific adjustment and stated that CMS lacks the statutory authority to uniformly reduce reimbursement for all 340B-eligible drugs paid under the OPPS. These commenters maintain that section 1833(t)(14) of the Act requires CMS to calculate and set payment rates for each specified covered outpatient drug. In other words, on a drug-by-drug basis.
Response: We disagree that section 1833(t)(14) of the Act requires CMS to calculate and set payment rates for each specified covered outpatient drug. While the statute indicates that data should be collected for specific drugs, it is not prescriptive regarding how that data should ultimately be used to set payment rates. Payment rates are already set on a drug-by-drug basis using the ASP methodology, and this will continue to be the manner in which payment rates for individual drugs are set. The percentage adjustment applied to the ASP (ASP plus six percent) has never been tailored to individual HCPCS codes; this policy mirrors that approach. Further, the proposed ASP percentage adjustment was volume-weighted to reflect the relative utilization and differing margins of individual drugs.
As stated in the proposed rule, it would not be practical to calculate a drug-specific payment rate for each NDC, and each HCPCS code, based on the survey data, as the survey-collected data is based on a snapshot in time and would not reflect future changes in average acquisition costs. Therefore, as drug prices change, we believe it is appropriate and reasonable to continue to update the calculated ASPs and then to reduce payments by an appropriate percentage of ASP to better align payment with the average cost of the drug.
Comment: Some commenters supported our alternative proposal to set OPPS payment for 340B-acquired drugs at ASP minus 28.0 percent based on 340B ceiling price data. Most of these commenters indicated that they supported neither alternative but that if CMS nonetheless proceeded with a payment adjustment that they preferred ASP minus 28 percent because an approach grounded in objective, regularly updated ceiling price data would be less disruptive than the survey-based methodology. Another commenter stated that this approach would be better because it relies on a more complete, independently maintained data source. Several commenters suggested that if we proceeded with the ASP minus 28 percent approach that we should weight it using Medicare claims volume for the applicable calendar year. A commenter urged CMS to more fully evaluate this alternative, which they contended avoided many of the response-rate and representativeness concerns expressed by commenters.
Response: We agree with commenters that our alternative approach would have several advantages compared to our proposed survey-data-based approach. A payment rate based on ceiling price data would be objective and could be updated annually with far less burden to hospitals and CMS than an annual survey. We also think that this approach is appropriate based on the survey results, which, as we noted previously, found that hospitals' survey-reported 340B acquisition costs were at least 28.9 percent below the mean ASP for drugs in all high-spending therapeutic classes (that is, those with more than $100 million in reported acquisition costs).
We thank the commenters for their comments regarding updating the ceiling price payment rate weighted by claims volume for the applicable calendar year, in this case 2025 claims for CY 2027 rulemaking, rather than claims data from the duration of the survey. CMS will consider this for future rulemaking, but for CY 2027 will calculate the 340B ceiling price data using claims data mirroring the survey timeframe.
Comment: A few commenters recommending the ASP minus 28 percent alternative suggested that we phase it in gradually over several years, which would provide us with the opportunity to provide additional drug-level information, evaluate actual claims experience, establish an appropriate payment for pharmacy and clinical infrastructure, and create hospital groupings that recognize safety-net, teaching, trauma, pediatric, and rural responsibilities. One of these commenters stated that such an approach would recognize CMS' legitimate interest in better aligning payment with acquisition cost without immediately adopting the largest reduction supported by an aggregate survey whose 340B hospital response rate and drug-level representativeness remain contested.
Response: We appreciate the commenters' suggestions to phase-in in our policy; however. as we stated previously, we believe that the payment misalignment that our proposed policy would address has been in effect for many years and it is important to implement this policy without delay now that we have conducted the required survey and have data clearly demonstrating that the existing payment rate for 340B-acquired drugs is so far out of line as a representative proxy for the cost of their acquisition.
Comment: Several commenters opposed our alternative proposal to set OPPS payment for 340B-acquired drugs at ASP minus 28.0 percent based on 340B ceiling price data. One of these commenters expressed confusion as to what feedback CMS might be requesting since, in their view, the Supreme Court's decision in AHA v. Becerra forecloses HHS from setting payment for 340B drugs based on “subjective measures.” In this commenter's view, under the statute, CMS can only vary payment by hospital group when it is using the survey data to set payment rates: “In AHA v. Becerra, the Supreme Court held that if HHS collects hospital acquisition cost survey data from hospitals, then HHS may use the data to set reimbursement rates equal to the average acquisition cost for the drug. . . . Importantly, in that circumstance, HHS may vary reimbursement rates by hospital group. While CMS conducted a survey for 2027, it is not proposing to use that survey data to set acquisition costs by hospital group; instead, it is using the survey as attempted cover to rely on what would otherwise be an improper source of data on which to base payment adjustments by hospital group.” (Internal quotation marks omitted.) Additionally, several ( printed page 70534) commenters stated that ASP minus 28 percent was not an acceptable substitute because a ceiling price is a statutory maximum, the highest price a manufacturer may charge a covered entity, not a measure of what hospitals actually pay or what it costs them to dispense a drug. One of these commenters opined that setting payment by reference to ceiling prices would convert a price cap into a presumed actual acquisition cost, which is not the “average acquisition cost for the drug” the statute directs CMS to determine. One commenter urged CMS not to adopt the alternative rate of ASP minus 28 percent because the proposed 33.4 percent reduction is derived from valid, newly collected hospital acquisition data and represents the most accurate market reality.
Response: We disagree that the statute or the Supreme Court's decision in AHA v. Becerra requires us to set payment rates using the hospital acquisition cost survey data as a precondition to vary payment by hospital group. Section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii)(I) of the Act requires the Secretary to “take into account” the hospital acquisition cost survey data. It does not require the Secretary to apply the actual data from the survey to set payment rates. We have taken into account the hospital acquisition cost survey data; indeed, it is our thorough analysis of that data that demonstrates (1) the clear and substantial discrepancy between current payment for 340B-acquired drugs and acquisition cost for 340B drugs that requires a prompt and reasonable solution, and (2) that a payment rate of ASP minus 28 percent would reflect a reasonable and conservative estimate of the average acquisition costs for 340B drugs for 340B hospitals given the survey results shows an average acquisition cost of ASP minus 33.4 percent. This is consistent with the approach we adopted in response to the GAO's survey in 2006. When the GAO conducted their survey and released their report, CMS did not use the survey data to directly set drug payment rates prospectively. Rather, CMS used that information to validate the appropriateness of ASP plus 6 percent as the Medicare payment rate. In its report, the GAO stated that “[t]o ensure that Medicare payments for SCOD products are based on sufficiently accurate data, we recommend that the Secretary . . . validate, on an occasional basis, manufacturers' reported drug ASPs as a measure of hospitals' acquisition costs using a survey of hospitals or other method that CMS determines to be similarly accurate and efficient.” [138] CMS conducted the survey and the survey demonstrated that (1) current Medicare payment for 340B-acquired drugs is not based on sufficiently accurate data, as evidenced by the nearly 40-percent discrepancy between average acquisition cost and Medicare payment; and (2) that ASP minus 28 percent would reflect a reasonable and conservative estimate of the discounts 340B hospitals receive on 340B drugs.
We acknowledge that 340B ceiling prices are the maximum prices that pharmaceutical manufacturers can charge hospitals participating in the 340B Program. However, we do not agree that renders them unsuitable to inform Medicare payment rates.
Comment: A few commenters stated that the existence of the two alternatives suggests that neither should be adopted. According to these commenters, the two alternatives constitute “materially different estimates” from Federal data sources, which underscore both the uncertainty surrounding the underlying analysis and the limitations of using a single national average discount assumption to establish payment rates for a highly diverse set of drugs and providers.
Response: We do not agree with commenters' assessment of the two alternatives. We acknowledge their differing natures; however, we do not believe that they signify uncertainty in our analysis or limitations in using a single national average discount to establish payment rates for 340B-acquired drugs. In fact, we believe that the relative uniformity of these two estimates of ASP minus 28.0 percent and ASP minus 33.4 percent augers for the validity and accuracy of these two estimates, with the ASP minus 28.0 percent estimate naturally and predictably reflecting a slightly more conservative estimate of the discounts 340B hospitals receive on 340B-acquired drugs.
Comment: A commenter preferred the proposed ASP minus 33.4 percent methodology over the alternative ASP minus 28 percent approach because it is grounded directly in observed hospital acquisition costs. The commenter observed that while an ASP minus 28 percent methodology might slightly lessen the fiscal impact of the revised policy, the acquisition-cost survey provides a more direct empirical foundation than an alternative derived from estimates of statutory ceiling prices.
Response: We agree with the commenter that the proposed ASP minus 33.4 percent methodology has several advantages in comparison to the ASP minus 28 percent alternative in that it is based on real world acquisition cost data and would more fully capture the discount hospitals are receiving. However, as previously discussed, we believe ceiling price payment methodology volume-weighted by OPPS claims data is a reasonable alternative, as it is based on objective data, can be updated regularly (at least annually, and perhaps quarterly in the future as we gain more experience with this process) with the release of new ceiling prices and new claims utilization data, and significantly diminishes the discrepancy between Medicare payment and hospital acquisition costs for these drugs. It is a reasonable, empirically based payment methodology and the accuracy of our estimate is reinforced by the survey finding similar, but slightly larger, average discounts for 340B drugs acquired by 340B hospitals.
After consideration of public comments received and after taking into account the hospital acquisition cost survey data, we are finalizing our alternative proposal to set OPPS payment for 340B-acquired drugs at ASP minus 28 percent based on 340B ceiling price data and we are revising 42 CFR 419.41(d) and adding a new paragraph (k) to implement this payment change. While we believe both alternatives to be excellent proxies for hospitals' acquisition costs for 340B-acquired drugs, we think that the virtues of setting the payment rate for 340B drugs acquired by 340B hospitals at ASP minus 28 percent based on the 340B ceiling data as validated by the ODACS outweigh the advantages of using the ASP minus 33.4 percent payment rate based on the survey data alone. ASP minus 28 percent is based on objective data, is a reasonable and conservative estimate of hospital 340B drug acquisition costs as validated by the ODACS, and is responsive to commenters' concerns that a payment rate of ASP minus 33.4 percent would result in too significant of a payment reduction and would inhibit beneficiary access to these drugs. ASP minus 28 percent is also in line with the minimum discount by major therapeutic class CMS found from the ODACS, where the acquisition costs varied from a high of ASP minus 28.8 percent to a low of ASP minus 71.4 percent. Additionally, our 95 percent confidence interval analyses of the survey data determined that acquisition costs fell between ASP minus 34.7 percent and ASP minus 32.3 percent. When including the IPW analysis, this 95 ( printed page 70535) percent confidence interval became ASP minus 34.3 to minus 32.1 percent. It additionally is in line with the average acquisition costs stratified by various hospital characteristics as shown in Table 70. Specifically, and as previously discussed, we assessed the survey data by drug acquisition volume, OPPS drug billing volume, hospital size (number of beds), geographic rurality, census region, teaching status, share of Medicare patients, disproportionate share percent, and hospital type. Through all of these different hospital characteristics, assessing both the mean and median results, the margin drops as low as ASP minus 39.7 percent, and as high as ASP minus 30.3 percent. Through these 96 permutations of the data, these tight ranges not only support the integrity of the survey results but also make the ceiling price alternative that we are adopting reasonable and should help alleviate any commenter concerns that the payment rate based on the survey data is inappropriate.
We note that in the event that our authority under section 1833(t)(14) of the Act was determined to not provide sufficient flexibility to utilize the 340B ceiling price data as validated by the ODACS to set a payment rate of ASP minus 28 percent for 340B-acquired drugs for CY 2027, we believe the payment rate of ASP minus 33.4 percent—as determined by the average 340B drug acquisition cost in the ODACS—to be a better, more accurate determination of such hospital acquisitions costs than our prior policy of ASP plus 6 percent.
4. Add-On Payment for 340B Drugs
Under the OPPS, Medicare pays separately payable drugs at rates that approximate their acquisition costs, such as at ASP or WAC. These drugs may also receive an add-on payment. Under the OPPS, section 1833(t)(14)(E) of the Act authorizes, but does not require, the Secretary to make an adjustment to payment rates for SCODs to take into account overhead and related expenses, such as pharmacy services and handling costs. Because we took a prudent approach in estimating the average acquisition costs for 340B-acquired drugs, we did not believe that it was necessary to establish an add-on for overhead and handling as we believed that a conservative estimate may already account for the costs of overhead. We also believed that hospitals would likely negotiate additional discounts that will render an additional add-on payment unnecessary. This approach also aligned with the requirement under section 1833(t)(14)(A)(iii) of the Act to pay at the average acquisition cost. Therefore, for CY 2027 and subsequent years, we proposed to pay for 340B drugs acquired under the 340B Program by 340B hospitals at ASP minus 33.4 percent with no add-on payment. We sought comment on our proposal to not include an add-on payment.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: A commenter supported our proposal not to provide an add-on. This commenter cautioned CMS about layering additional payments onto the survey-derived amount without clear evidence that they represent costs not already captured in the methodology. The commenter found our proposal reasonable “insofar as the underlying acquisition-cost estimate already provides an appropriate approximation of hospitals' costs associated with obtaining these drugs. A separate adjustment should require evidence of a distinct and material expense rather than become another mechanism through which the gap between Medicare reimbursement and acquisition cost gradually reemerges.”
Response: We thank the commenter for their support.
Comment: Many commenters objected to our proposal not to include an add-on payment for overhead and handling and faulted our proposed payment methodology for failing to capture all of the costs associated with furnishing a drug and complying with the 340B Program. Commenters listed many of these expenses, including acquiring, storing, preparing, administering, and monitoring medications, implementing software, hiring additional staff, inventory management, infusion center infrastructure and clinical staffing, medication safety and quality programs, information technology and electronic health record infrastructure, regulatory and compliance requirements, sterile compounding facilities, USP compliance, hazardous drug protections, medication-use technology, waste handling and disposal, shortage mitigation efforts, diversion prevention programs, audit readiness activities, 24/7 clinical support, cybersecurity protections, accreditation standards, emergency preparedness capabilities, dedicated 340B pharmacy staff, split-billing software, annual licensing fees, daily reconciliation of 340B and non-340B inventory to prevent diversion, preparation for HRSA audits and responses to manufacturer audits, with associated legal and compliance costs, as well as ongoing regulatory monitoring, cold-chain management, nuclear medicine technologists, nurses, and multidisciplinary care coordination, hot lab, infusion, dedicated bathroom infrastructure, dose calibration, decay correction, and radiation safety oversight. A commenter emphasized the importance of the add-on payment for hospitals dispensing high-cost cellular and gene therapy products, including CAR-T therapies, that require specialized apheresis and cell-processing capacity; chain-of-custody and chain-of-identity protocols; and compliance with many additional requirements.
Many commenters disagreed with our rationale for not establishing an add-on. In the proposed rule we stated that an add-on was unnecessary because (1) we took a prudent approach in estimating the average acquisition costs for 340B-acquired drugs and we believe that that prudent estimate of acquisition cost may already account for overhead and (2) we believe that hospitals will likely negotiate additional discounts. A commenter characterized the decision as arbitrary and capricious, stating that CMS provides no justification for the exclusion and “merely states that its cost estimate may already account for the costs of overhead, a weak statement that undermines confidence in the adequacy of the resulting payment rate.” Several commenters shared their view that CMS' assumption that hospitals will likely negotiate additional discounts was inconsistent with market realities. A commenter indicated that in their experience, voluntary discounts for high-cost drugs were rare, particularly those for which a limited number of manufacturers dominate the market. A few commenters alleged that CMS's assumption is internally inconsistent with the underlying premise of the proposed payment methodology. These commenters stated that we propose to establish a payment rate based on survey data that we describe as representative and sufficiently reliable to estimate average acquisition cost. These commenters then ask, if the survey is statistically valid and accurately measures acquisition costs, how can CMS simultaneously justify the absence of an overhead add-on by speculating that hospitals may receive undocumented and unmeasured discounts beyond those reflected in the survey? “Either the Survey accurately captures acquisition costs or it does not,” a commenter stated. A few commenters alleged that, in setting the payment rate, CMS failed to account for how cost structures vary dramatically across different types of hospitals. ( printed page 70536)
Many commenters emphasized that acquisition costs and overhead costs are two separate measures and that in setting the payment rate CMS conflated the reported acquisition costs with overhead costs. A commenter pointed out that the current payment rate of ASP plus 6 percent contains the average sales price (a proxy for acquisition cost) plus a 6 percent add-on for overhead costs and that in the survey, CMS collected only a hospital's total net acquisition cost for a drug defined as “the total amount paid by the hospital inclusive of all discounts, rebates, and price concessions applicable at the NDC level.” The commenter stated that hospitals were not instructed to report any additional costs that they incurred to administer the drugs, such as overhead, pharmacy services, and handling costs.
Many commenters alleged that not including a 6 percent add-on for 340B drugs would arbitrarily create a payment differential for overhead costs compared to non-340B drugs that is not supported by the survey or other analysis. Another commenter stated that the proposal is flawed because the agency is proposing to continue providing an add-on payment to hospitals exempt from its proposed payment policy, but not for hospitals subject to its proposed policy. In doing so, the commenter states, the agency recognizes that overhead costs are real and legitimate components of Medicare payment policy for some hospitals, but not for others. “CMS provides no rationale for why the same overhead, pharmacy operations, drug handling, storage, inventory management, compliance, billing, and patient care costs disappear when the same drug is acquired by a 340B hospital subject to its proposed payment policy. Excluding any add-on payment from the proposed 340B payment rate therefore creates an arbitrary and internally inconsistent payment policy that recognizes overhead costs for some hospitals and some drugs, while ignoring those same costs for others.” Another commenter alleged that the proposed policy creates a logical disconnect between reimbursement for drugs at 340B and non-340B sites. “Payment policy for the former would reject the need for an add-on that covers overhead costs, and the latter would recognize the need to reimburse these costs. At no point does CMS make a case for this distinction.” Another commenter requested CMS to explain why comparable operational costs are recognized for non-340B drugs but not for 340B-acquired drugs and radiopharmaceuticals.
Response: We acknowledge the many costs that are associated with the delivery of a drug; however, as we have explained, we believe that, due to our prudent approach in determining an average acquisition cost, our proposed payment amount for 340B-acquired drugs does not support CMS exercising its discretion to include an add-on or adjustment in payment for overhead costs. Many of the costs mentioned by commenters are standard operating costs of hospitals and healthcare facilities and are not necessarily related to the cost of the drug. Additionally, as we are finalizing the alternative ASP minus 28 percent payment rate, a significantly conservative average acquisition cost, it is not necessary to provide an add-on. Finally, an add-on percentage, such as a 6 percent add-on to ASP, can create incentives for some providers to choose higher-priced products over lower-priced products even when the two products are clinically equivalent.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to not include an add-on payment for 340B-acquired drugs.
5. 340B Payment Policy for Drugs for Which ASP Is Unavailable
Section 1847A of the Act establishes the average sales price (ASP) methodology, which provides the amount payable for drugs and biologicals described in section 1842(o)(1)(C) of the Act furnished on or after January 1, 2005. Based on this, our historic policy has been to pay for most drugs at ASP plus 6 percent. There are some situations, however, where it is not possible to pay ASP because, for example, a drug is sufficiently new so there is no sales data available upon which to derive an average. In these situations, our historic policy has been to pay for the drug according to the following hierarchy: In general, if ASP information is not available, payment is based on the WAC with WAC plus 6 percent. If WAC information also is not available, then payment is based on AWP with 95 percent of AWP being paid. If AWP is not available, then payment is based on Mean Unit Cost (MUC). And if MUC is not available, then payment is based on the invoice price.
Consistent with this policy, starting in CY 2027, we proposed that payment for 340B drugs when ASP is unavailable mirrors CMS's historic payment policies for drugs paid under OPPS. If ASP information is not available, payment is based on the WAC, with WAC minus 33.4 percent. If WAC information also is not available, we proposed a payment rate of 59.69 [139] percent of AWP. This percent was calculated by first reducing the original 95 percent of AWP price by 6 percent to generate a value that is similar to WAC with no percentage markup. Then we applied the 33.4 percent reduction WAC-similar AWP value to obtain the 59.69 percent of AWP, which is similar to either ASP minus 33.4 percent or WAC minus 33.4 percent. For 340B drugs paid based on MUC, we proposed to continue to pay them at 100 percent of MUC. These MUC-based payments are calculated based on hospital claims data, which already account for hospital acquisition costs and do not need to be discounted further. Similarly, we proposed to continue to pay for invoice priced 340B drugs at the invoice amount as the invoice price amount should already reflect the 340B discount. We sought comment on this proposal.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: One commenter requested clarification as to whether we are proposing to pay MUC only for 340B drugs for which ASP is unavailable or are we also proposing to pay for 340B drugs for which ASP is available but is paid under the MUC under non-340B settings. Another commenter noted that while ASP minus 33.4 percent appears to be higher than most proposed MUC-based rates for CY 2027, applying different reimbursement methodologies to 340B-acquired drugs, biologics, and diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals without pass-through status that are subject to MUC-based payment may create additional confusion for hospitals. The commenter requested that CMS provide additional clarification, as needed, in the CY 2027 OPPS Final Rule.
Response: If ASP information is not available, payment is based on the WAC. If WAC information also is not available, payment is based on AWP. If AWP is not available, then payment is based on arithmetic MUC. If MUC is not available, then payment is based on invoice pricing. However, certain products, such as nonpass-through diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals with claims data, will continue to be paid based on arithmetic MUC as discussed in this final rule with comment period. MUC-based payments are calculated based on hospital claims data, including 340B and non-340B drugs, which ( printed page 70537) already account for hospital acquisition costs and do not need to be discounted further. If we were to discount this payment rate, then we would be accounting for 340B discounts twice.
After consideration of these public comments, we are finalizing our payment hierarchy for when ASP is not available as proposed: If ASP information is not available, payment will be based on the WAC; if WAC information is not available, payment will be based on AWP; if AWP is not available, payment will be based on MUC; and if MUC is not available, payment will be based on the invoice price. However, given our adoption of the proposed alternative of ASP minus 28 percent, we are not finalizing the reduction amounts that we proposed for WAC and AWP. Consistent with the reduction amount we are adopting, we are finalizing WAC minus 28 percent and 64.53 percent of AWP. We are finalizing our proposal to pay 100 percent of MUC for 340B drugs paid based on MUC and the invoice amount for invoiced priced 340B drugs as proposed.
We proposed to apply our proposed policy to pay for drugs acquired under the 340B Program at ASP minus 33.4 percent to all separately payable drugs, biologicals, biosimilars and radiopharmaceuticals acquired under the 340B Program. This approach would establish a uniform payment policy consistent with our historic OPPS payment policy of paying the same payment rate for SCODs and non-SCODs. We noted our proposal to apply this policy to separately payable drugs and biologicals that are not SCODs was a policy proposal rather than a statutory requirement. We note that the survey included both SCODs and drugs and biologicals that we have historically treated as SCODs for payment purposes. We have treated non-SCOD drugs as SCODs for payment purposes since CY 2006. We sought comment on this proposal.
The payment policy would not apply to vaccines, as they are excluded from the 340B Program; drugs with transitional pass-through payment status, which are paid under section 1833(t)(6)(D) of the Act; and non-opioid pain management drugs as defined under section 1833(t)(16)(G) of the Act, as we believe reducing payment for those drugs would be inconsistent with statutory instructions on payment amount for those qualifying products. As previously described in the information collection request approved by OMB under the PRA, CMS may continue to validate the results of this survey on a periodic basis; for example, perhaps as often as every 4 years. We sought comment on this proposal. Specifically, we sought comment on the proposal that the policy to pay for drugs acquired under the 340B Program at ASP minus 33.4 percent would apply to all separately payable drugs, biologicals, biosimilars and radiopharmaceuticals acquired under the 340B Program, and would not apply to vaccines, drugs with transitional pass-through payment status and non-opioid pain management drugs.
Additionally, as we proposed to apply a single discount factor to the ASP for 340B-acquired drugs in lieu of calculating individual acquisition cost amounts for 340B-acquired drugs, we believed it was appropriate to apply this payment adjustment using the single discount factor to existing and new drugs that are paid under the OPPS.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Several commenters stated that CMS lacks the statutory authority to apply a 340B-differentiated rate to drugs that are not SCODs. These commenters point to section 1833(t)(14)(B) of the Act which defines a SCOD as “a covered outpatient drug (as defined in section 1927(k)(2)) for which a separate ambulatory payment classification group (APC) has been established and that is (I) a radiopharmaceutical agent; or (II) a drug or biological for which payment was made [on a pass-through basis] on or before December 31, 2002” and excludes drugs that first received pass-through payment on or after January 1, 2003. These commenters state that if CMS wants to apply the ASP minus 33.4 percent rate to separately payable drugs not meeting this definition ( i.e., drugs CMS has historically treated as SCODs), then CMS must identify, drug by drug or class by class, the statutory authority on which that differential rests. A commenter requested that CMS enumerate in the final rule which HCPCS codes CMS treats as SCODs and state the authority applied to each separately payable drug outside that definition.
Response: We disagree that we lack the statutory authority to apply our proposed payment policy to drugs that we have historically treated as SCODs. We note that in the event that our authority under section 1833(t) of the Act was determined not to be sufficient to adjust payment for 340B-acquired SCODs to ASP minus 28 percent, we would continue to apply an adjusted payment rate for 340B-acquirednon-SCODs. Similarly, we note that in the event that our authority under the Act was determined not to be sufficient to adjust payment for 340B-acquired non-SCODs, we would continue to apply an adjusted payment rate for 340B-acquired SCODs.
Comment: Most commenters who commented on our proposal not to apply the payment adjustment to vaccines, drugs with transitional pass-through payment status, and qualifying non-opioid pain management drugs under section 1833(t)(16)(G) of the Act supported it. One commenter thanked CMS for recognizing that failing to exempt NOPAIN Act-qualifying drugs would undercut—or severely limit—the underlying policy goal of increasing use of and access to non-addictive pain management approaches. Similarly, another commenter expressed strong support for our proposal not to apply the payment adjustment to qualifying non-opioid pain management drugs under section 1833(t)(16)(G) of the Act because applying an additional 340B payment adjustment to these products would be inconsistent with the statutory framework governing payment for eligible non-opioid treatments. The commenter stated that finalizing the exclusion would help preserve the integrity of the separate payment policy established by Congress, ensure that qualifying non-opioid products continue to be reimbursed in a manner consistent with the statutory methodology applicable to them and help ensure Medicare beneficiaries retain access to clinically appropriate alternatives to opioids.
Response: We thank commenters for their support.
Comment: A commenter requested that CMS confirm that the proposed policy does not apply to 340B-acquired diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals with pass-through status.
Response: Please see section V.A. of this final rule with comment period for discussion of pass-through payment for drugs, biologicals, biosimilars, and radiopharmaceuticals.
