Response: We appreciate the input and feedback from commenters. Once again, we emphasize that this is an interim first step to a broader payment policy for SaMS. We intended to preserve current payment rates for these services as much as possible for CY 2027 while assigning these services to new technology APCs. Many commenters claimed resources costs for these services are higher than the proposed payment rates and that they are concerned about beneficiary access to these clinical meaningful services. We are committed to developing a comprehensive and consistent approach for these technologies and our objective remains to have this new payment strategy align with CMS's mission to increase quality, improve health, reduce costs, and strengthen the healthcare system. We proposed to maintain current payment rates as much as possible for these services that we designated as SaMS as we moved them to new technology APCs and we continue to believe that that is the right approach. We thank the commenters again for their input and we will consider this feedback as part of our deliberations regarding our long-term payment methodology for SaMS.
Comment: Commenters were very supportive of the proposed new “O1” status indicator for SaMS. Commenters opposed mirroring the payment specifications of the new “O1” status indicator using “T,” which would apply multiple procedure discounting to SaMS. Several commenters explained that the rationale behind multiple-procedure discounting does not apply to SaMS because, unlike other non-software based services which share physical resources, and therefore, subsequent procedures are less expensive, SaMS do not rely on shared resources. Commenters noted that algorithmic services do not rely on these shared resources: when two distinct algorithms are run on a single claim, each represents an independent service with its own development, validation, and computational costs, not a marginal add-on to a shared setup. Commenters further explained that separate payment is appropriate because SaMS tests are distinct diagnostic services that are separately ordered, performed after specimen collection or after or concurrently with an imaging scan, and reported to inform subsequent treatment planning. Commenters also believed it would not be appropriate to address program integrity concerns through the status indicator specifications and thought they would be better addressed through the claims-level tracking that the “O1” status indicator itself enables, together with medical-necessity review.
Response: We agree with commenters, at this time, that these services are currently furnished as separate, independent services and that payment should reflect that for our interim maintenance policy. Therefore, we are creating the proposed new status indicator “O1” and use the same payment specifications as status indicator “S” to allow for separate payment without multiple procedure discounting.
Comment: A commenter requested that CMS state that SaMS designation is a payment-category designation and does not itself establish coverage or medical necessity.
Response: We appreciate the comment. As we have consistently stated in past OPPS/ASC final rules with comment period (see, for example, 87 FR 71879 and 88 FR 81660 through 81661), the fact that a drug, device, procedure or service is assigned a HCPCS code and a payment rate under the OPPS does not imply coverage by the Medicare program, but indicates only how the product, procedure, or service may be paid if covered by the program. Therefore, SaMS designation and assignment to status indicator “O1” and a new technology APC does not imply coverage.
Comment: A few commenters requested that we revise the status indicator of certain HCPCS codes that we proposed to continue to always or conditionally packaged (assigned to “N” or “Q1”, respectively) for CY 2027 to status indicator “O1”. For example, we received comments that did not support our proposal to maintain assignment to status indicator “Q1” for CPT codes 92227, 92228, 0902T, 0904T, and 9044T. Commenters explained that conditionally packaging these services risks providing inadequate or no separate payment for technologies that CMS has itself determined warrant recognition as a distinct category of medical services.
Response: We thank the commenters for their input. As provided in our proposal, our intention behind this policy is to provide an interim policy that minimizes payment disruption for CY 2027. Because these codes are currently assigned to status indicator “Q1,” we do not believe that finalizing to maintain the status indicator assignments for CY 2027 would cause payment disruptions. As such, we are finalizing the status indicators of the HCPCS codes we proposed to assign to Q1 or N as proposed. We refer readers to Table 84 for the clinical APC assignments and status indicators for the relevant HCPCS codes. The final CY 2027 payment rates can be found in Addendum B to this final rule with comment period via the internet on the CMS website. In addition, we refer readers to Addendum D1 to this final ( printed page 70621) rule with comment period for the status indicator meanings for all codes reported under the OPPS. Addendum D1 can also be found via the internet on the CMS website.
Comment: We received a comment seeking clarification regarding the process for technologies that receive FDA clearance outside of the rulemaking cycle to become designated as a SaMS and assigned to status indicator “O1”.
Response: SaMS that receive FDA clearance for their devices outside of the rulemaking cycle would receive the same treatment as other services that receive FDA clearance for their associated devices outside of the rulemaking cycle; CMS would use our normal quarterly coding processes for these services. We note that although the services we have designated as SaMS in this section of this final rule with comment period (section X.B.1.), are required to have FDA marketing authorization to receive Medicare payment, “SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests,” which are described in the following section of this final rule with comment period (section X.B.2.), currently do not require FDA marketing authorization in order to receive payment.
Comment: We received many comments with ideas and information for us to consider while developing a proposed longer-term methodology for future rulemaking. Below is a brief summary of several ideas we received. Many commenters urged CMS to establish a permanent, predictable, and distinct reimbursement pathway for SaMS, cautioning that inadequate reimbursement could push practices toward less precise, outdated treatment planning approaches. To support this longer-term work, several commenters recommended that CMS act now to build better data infrastructure, particularly by creating a dedicated cost center and revenue code so that hospitals can accurately report SaMS-related costs, such as licensing, implementation, training, and other fees, rather than folding them into existing departmental cost centers designed for other purposes, including imaging. Commenters also called for ongoing transparency and collaboration between CMS, physician specialty societies, and industry interested parties throughout the policy development process, along with clearer communication about the expected timeline for a more comprehensive framework.
On payment design, some suggested differentiating SaMS by clinical function ( e.g., computer-aided detection, diagnosis, or triage) using objective criteria such as FDA clearance, clinical validation, and peer-reviewed evidence of impact on patient management. Many commenters discussed the types of costs we should consider for payment and emphasized that any methodology must account for the full cost of safe deployment, including integration, cybersecurity, monitoring, and clinician oversight, not just vendor licensing fees. Commenters were divided on using the new technology APC pathway as a longer-term solution, with some advocating for new technology APC assignment for at least five years, while others noted this approach may not adequately address the unique, market-driven pricing dynamics of SaMS. Finally, several commenters offered perspectives on value-based payment approaches, with some encouraging CMS to weigh demonstrated clinical outcomes and others cautioning that reliable outcome-based payment requires stronger claims-level tracking and verification of human oversight rather than assumptions about its effectiveness.
Response: We appreciate the commenters' thoughtful discussion and ideas. We will consider the comments received as we prepare potential policy proposals for CY 2028. We welcome continued engagement from interested parties regarding future payment methodologies. Future payment methodologies for SaMS would go through the annual rulemaking process to ensure proper engagement with the public.
2. SaMS Analyses Performed on Laboratory Tests
In recent years, we have seen an increase in laboratory tests that combine laboratory analyses, such as genomic sequencing or immunoassays, with computer algorithms to produce a clinical test result. The AMA CPT Editorial Panel created a category called Multi-Analyte Assays with Algorithmic Analysis (MAAA's), to categorize test codes that combined laboratory analyses with computer algorithms to generate clinical information. More recently, however, we are seeing the development of distinct algorithmic analyses alone with distinct CPT codes.
For example, when the genomic sequencing of an individual is performed, this sequencing will likely only need to be performed once by a laboratory. However, once the genomic sequence has been generated, the subsequent algorithmic analyses of that sequence data can be performed an infinite number of times to produce a wide range of results and/or diagnostic or risk-related information. These secondary analyses of original genomic sequences can be proprietary and unique to a single laboratory but could also be conducted at a range of settings. For purposes of this final rule with comment period, we are referring to subsequent stand-alone algorithmic analyses as “SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests”.
As discussed in the proposed rule, currently, certain SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests are treated as clinical diagnostic laboratory tests (CDLTs) and paid under the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (CLFS) (91 FR 41925). Section 1861(s) of the Act specifies items and services included as “medical and other health services” under Part B, including diagnostic X-ray tests, diagnostic laboratory tests, and other diagnostic tests as described in section 1861(s)(3) of the Act. Sections 1833(h) and 1834A of the Act and the implementing regulations at 42 CFR part 414, subpart G, set forth the CLFS rate setting methodologies for CDLTs. We stated in the proposed rule that we do not believe it is appropriate to consider these secondary algorithmic analyses, when performed alone, to be CDLTs or establish CLFS payment rates for these analyses because we believe these secondary algorithmic analyses may not currently require laboratory services or entities, regulated by CLIA, to perform them. Our position is that the secondary analyses, which have distinct CPT codes,[174] are “other diagnostic tests” under section 1861(s)(3) of the Act as opposed to “diagnostic laboratory tests.” As noted previously, Medicare will not pay for CDLTs on the CLFS unless they are furnished by laboratories that meet applicable certification requirements. Tests that examine materials derived from the human body are assigned to and paid under the CLFS only when furnished by such certified laboratories in accordance with 42 CFR 410.32(d). Because SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests are downstream evaluations of the data generated by a prior laboratory test, which are described by distinct CPT codes, an entity that performs only algorithmic analyses of previously ( printed page 70628) sequenced data may not meet the definition of a “laboratory” under 42 CFR 493.2 or qualify for payment under CLFS. We believe SaMS that evaluate data generated by a prior laboratory test should not be treated as CDLTs for Medicare payment purposes.
As discussed in the proposed rule, we are also concerned that paying for these analyses based on existing CLFS payment methodologies may create significant vulnerabilities for the Medicare program, due to the lack of data transparency and CDLTs not being subject to beneficiary cost-sharing or budget neutrality. 42 CFR 414.508 outlines the rate setting methodologies CMS uses to set payment rates for new tests on the CLFS. Under § 414.508(b), CMS determines the payment amount based on either crosswalking or gapfilling methodologies until applicable information is available to establish a payment amount under the methodology described in § 414.507(b). Crosswalking is used if it is determined that a new CDLT is comparable to an existing test, multiple existing test codes, or a portion of an existing test code. Gapfilling is used when no comparable existing CDLT is available. Public consultation for payment for a new clinical diagnostic laboratory test is required in determining payment amounts, receiving public comments and recommendations (and data on which the recommendations are based) as well as recommendations from the Medicare Advisory Panel on Clinical Diagnostic Laboratory Tests (CDLTs) per § 414.506. A significant challenge to the rate setting process for CMS is receiving transparent data from laboratories outlining resource costs of a test, particularly for the algorithmic portions of tests that are combined with other analytes. In the past, laboratories have explained to CMS that the algorithmic components of laboratory tests are highly proprietary and details cannot be shared. Thus, CMS has worked with the limited information available on the details of methods or resources for the algorithmic portions of tests or analyses and has thus far relied on other laboratory methods provided in the CPT descriptor ( i.e., NGS sequencing, RT-PCR, or DNA methylation analysis). As CMS has gathered more information on SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests, we now believe that since these analyses are entirely computer-based, comparison based on laboratory methodologies is not appropriate. We believe that these analyses are substantially similar to other SaMS already paid under the OPPS. Additionally, in contrast to the OPPS, the CLFS generally does not include beneficiary cost-sharing or budget neutrality adjustments, which limits transparency regarding pricing and creates challenges for ensuring appropriate valuation of these services.
CMS has an interest in ensuring that services that are fundamentally similar are paid for and treated in the same way, regardless of the setting of care in which the service is furnished. Since we believe SaMS perform algorithmic analyses on previously generated data, we believe SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests are substantively similar to other SaMS technologies that are currently paid under the OPPS. Accordingly, we believe that whether the SaMS performs algorithmic analyses of an imaging test ( e.g. CT scan) or whether it performs an algorithmic analysis on data generated from a laboratory test, all algorithmic analyses should be treated consistently from a payment perspective. We believe that this uniform approach for SaMS technologies would promote stability and predictability in payment for similar services.
Finally, we note that CMS and CDC issued a Request for Information (RFI) on July 16, 2026, regarding CLIA regulations, the results of which may be used to help inform the agencies as to what types of action, if any, should be taken to update the existing CLIA regulations through future comment and rulemaking (91 FR 43586). The RFI closed for comments on September 15, 2026. CMS may refine SaMS payment and policies based on RFI responses and make changes in future rulemaking.
For CY 2027, as an interim first step to address concerns described above, we proposed to assign 10 HCPCS codes describing various SaMS analysis performed on laboratory tests to new technology APCs under the OPPS, using the latest available CLFS data to crosswalk to new technology APCs with payment rates that closely approximate the current CY 2026 CLFS payment rates for these codes. We note that SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests would not currently require FDA marketing authorization in order to receive payment under OPPS. SaMS payment policies may be refined in future rulemaking. We explained that the proposed payment rates for SaMS performed on prior laboratory tests cannot be expected to align exactly with current CLFS payment rates because assignment to new technology APCs is based on established cost bands rather than individual test-specific payment amounts. For example, if a HCPCS code is currently paid $430.17 under the CLFS, the appropriate new technology APC assignment under this proposal would be APC 1506 (New Technology—Level 6 ($401-$500)), which has a standardized payment rate of $450.50, rather than receiving a payment rate that exactly matches the current CLFS amount. We noted that, under this proposal, SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests would be paid separately by being assigned to new technology APCs with the newly proposed status indicator “O1” (Software as a Medical Service, Paid under OPPS; separate APC payment) for CY 2027. These 10 HCPCS codes were identified based on the CPT descriptor for the code. We noted that, if there were no laboratory methods included in the code descriptor, and only an algorithmic analysis was described, we identified the code as a SaMS analysis performed on a laboratory test. We invited public comment on this proposed list and any other similar analyses that should be removed from the CLFS and paid under the OPPS.
In addition, for CY 2027 and subsequent years, we proposed to assign any new SaMS analyses performed on laboratory test codes to new technology APCs for payment under the OPPS. We requested public comment on these proposals, including the list of 10 HCPCS codes that we identified as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests and any additional HCPCS codes that we should designate as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests and pay under the OPPS rather than the CLFS. We stated that CMS may finalize a policy that includes such payment for additional HCPCS codes in the final rule based on public comment.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Some commenters, including large cancer treatment centers, supported our proposal to establish a payment methodology for software-based analyses performed on laboratory tests distinct from the underlying laboratory test. These commenters supported migrating software-based analyses performed on laboratory tests from payment under the CLFS to payment under the OPPS and agreed that such analyses are better characterized as “other diagnostic tests.” Commenters added that this policy correctly recognizes algorithmic re-analysis of previously obtained data as a separately payable clinical service. In addition, commenters expressed support for establishing a consistent, cross-setting payment framework for algorithmic analyses, citing that this policy seeks to adapt and evolve with ( printed page 70629) changing healthcare environments. The commenters noted that it is especially critical that this payment policy evolve to reflect the value and resource costs of these technologies.
Response: We thank the commenters for their support and note that we will consider these comments as we continue to refine this payment policy.
Comment: Some commenters, including independent laboratories, supported our proposal but requested that CMS develop the payment methodology transparently, and ensure the payment for algorithm-driven services rests on evidence of clinical benefit. Commenters requested that CMS establish a payment mechanism for these services when the patient is not seen in a hospital outpatient department, noting that as proposed, the framework would leave no payment mechanism for a substantial share of medically necessary testing. Commenters also requested that CMS assign substantively comparable specimen-based algorithmic analyses to consistent new technology APCs and state the basis for APC assignment, and that CMS establish a defined, confidential process through which laboratories may submit cost and clinical outcomes data to support valuation as CMS develops a more comprehensive payment methodology. One commenter supported the proposal but requested that CMS defer changes to CLFS payment for algorithm-only laboratory analyses until the necessary coding, regulatory, and operational infrastructure has been established.
Response: We appreciate the suggestion to be transparent and thoughtful in the implementation of this policy. We believe that publicly proposing this policy in the proposed rule, inviting comments, and addressing those comments in this rule has made this process transparent. We also appreciate the recommendation to evaluate the clinical benefit of SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. We remind readers that our goal in this rulemaking cycle is to establish the category of SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests and the general payment mechanism for those services under the OPPS. Regarding a request to establish a separate confidential process through which laboratories may submit cost and clinical data, we remind commenters that we are available to meet with interested parties where information may be shared with CMS. However, because payment rates are finalized through the notice-and-comment rulemaking process, which requires providing the underlying reasoning for our proposals and final policy, establishing a separate confidential process would not be compatible with the existing rulemaking process. Further, finalizing this policy would not eliminate Medicare payment for these services, or prohibit certain facilities from billing Medicare, but rather, it would define how these services would be paid under the OPPS. For the purposes of maintaining stability, particularly for the HCPCS codes we proposed to remove from the CLFS and place in an APC category, we chose to assign APC levels based on the CY 2026 CLFS payment rates to avoid any considerable payment disruption. As we continue to develop this policy, we will consider possible methods for evaluating the APC assignment for new SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. We do not believe that it is appropriate to delay the movement of SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests from the CLFS to the OPPS, given the speed at which SaMS technologies are developing and the goal of having a consistent policy across payment systems for similar services. These services will be paid for under existing and well-established Medicare payment mechanisms, depending on the place of service (that is, hospital outpatient departments or physician offices).
Comment: A few commenters, specifically large laboratory associations, requested that we not finalize the policy as proposed. Commenters generally believed that CMS should engage with the laboratory community more closely prior to finalizing payment changes for SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. Commenters specifically expressed concerns that the proposed policy could inadvertently create duplicate or inconsistent payment pathways and fragment integrated laboratory services by separating algorithmic analyses from the laboratory responsible for validation, quality, clinical interpretation, and reporting. Several commenters expressed concerns regarding the implications of introducing beneficiary cost sharing for services that generally are not subject to cost sharing under the CLFS if this policy were to be finalized. One commenter explained that, if CMS is concerned about unregulated software vendors billing Medicare, CMS should condition Medicare payment for designated SaMS laboratory services on performance by a CLIA-certified, appropriately accredited laboratory.
Response: We acknowledge the commenters' concerns, and we will continue to consider them while we implement the policy. Regarding cost sharing, we acknowledge that while cost sharing shifts some costs to beneficiaries, it also encourages greater efficiency by providers and more economical delivery of medically necessary services, which would contain unnecessary growth in Medicare spending long-term to the benefit of both Medicare and beneficiaries.
We disagree with concerns that this final policy would fragment integrated laboratory services, as this policy would apply to HCPCS codes that already recognize a distinct SaMS analysis component. To ensure that this policy impacts HCPCS codes describing the secondary analyses only, we requested public comment on the list of HCPCS codes we proposed to designate as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. As discussed further below, based on public comments received, HCPCS codes describing integrated services, meaning those codes that describe both the wet lab and SaMS secondary analyses, were not finalized for payment under this policy for CY 2027. These HCPCS codes would continue to be paid under the CLFS.
Concerns about billing and regulations regarding vendors of SaMS analyses are outside of the scope of this final rule with comment period.
While we understand the commenters' concerns, we believe that the proposed policy provides a uniform payment pathway for SaMS that should be implemented for CY 2027. We continue to maintain that paying for SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests under the CLFS may create significant vulnerabilities for the Medicare program, due to the challenges in receiving transparent data regarding the algorithms themselves and CDLTs on the CLFS generally not being subject to beneficiary cost-sharing or budget neutrality. As mentioned above, we believe SaMS technologies generally should be treated and paid for consistently across the Medicare program because these algorithm-based services are functionally equivalent, despite differences in the type of clinical service or data. For example, both SaMS currently paid under the OPPS and SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests perform algorithm-based analyses on existing data. We anticipate that resource costs may be similar between these kinds of services. For SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests, assigning them to new technology APCs under the OPPS means similar algorithm-based services will be billed and paid for under the same payment system. We will continue to engage the broader laboratory community in further dialogue as we consider potential ( printed page 70630) refinements to this policy in future rulemaking.
Comment: Some commenters, especially large laboratory associations, asked CMS to not finalize its proposal to reassign SaMS analyses performed on prior laboratory tests to new technology APCs under the OPPS and to continue paying for these as CDLTs on the CLFS. A few commenters urged CMS to exempt current and future software-based laboratory tests from this proposed policy and only designate the proposed tests as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests.
Response: We appreciate these comments but believe it is important for SaMS-based technologies to be treated consistently across the Medicare program, rather than establishing distinct payment policies for similar SaMS depending on whether the analysis is performed on an imaging service or on a laboratory test.
Comment: Commenters generally expressed concern that the proposed framework to distinguish SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests from other laboratory tests would be challenging to apply in practice. Commenters stated that these services have generally been classified and paid as CDLTs under the CLFS, reflecting longstanding treatment from CMS, the AMA CPT process, and the FDA. Commenters expressed concern regarding using CPT code descriptors to determine which HCPCS codes should be designated as a SaMS analyses performed on a laboratory test since descriptors do not always indicate whether activities, such as slide preparation or immunostaining, are included in the reported service. Commenters explained that although SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests are defined as being both separate from specimen examination and entirely computer-based, several of the examples CMS identified appear to involve wet lab components, creating uncertainty regarding how the criteria would be operationalized, and that as a result, interested parties may face difficulty determining whether a given service qualifies as a purely algorithmic analysis or should continue to be treated as a laboratory test including wet lab processes. Commenters requested that CMS provide additional guidance and examples to support consistent classification and payment for these services.
Response: Medicare utilizes the description of services as provided by the HCPCS code descriptors in determining appropriate payment. For the proposed policy, we identified services listed on the CLFS that indicated algorithmic analysis in the CPT long descriptor and in the description of intraservice work (as provided by AMA in its valuation of CPT codes) and proposed to treat those services as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. Specifically, we considered code descriptors that included phrases such as “augmentative algorithmic analysis” or “previously established sequence,” as we believed that these indicated that the code described SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. We requested public comments on the proposed list of codes, understanding that we may have inadvertently omitted certain codes or included codes that do not solely describe subsequent, computer-based analyses as intended.
We appreciate the comments regarding the proposed list of codes. In this final rule with comment period, we have removed a few HCPCS codes from the proposed list, based on an additional understanding of the code descriptors and public comments received, but we retained the HCPCS codes that contained phrases such as “augmentative algorithmic analysis” or “previously established sequence” which we discuss in further detail below. We believe that the finalized list of HCPCS codes being reassigned from the CLFS to new technology APCs under the OPPS is limited to those that are entirely computer-based secondary analyses and do not include specimen examination performed as part of the wet lab component.
Comment: Commenters requested that CMS include additional specificity into the SaMS definition to ensure that technologies and services with meaningful differences, such as algorithm-only laboratory-developed tests, laboratory Software as a Medical Device, and imaging Software as a Medical Device, are not treated as equivalent for payment purposes. One commenter proposed that CMS limit the services included in this policy to algorithmic reanalysis of a prior laboratory test's reported results, and exclude any service that examines a patient's specimen, physical or digitized, or that measures a defined analyte from that specimen.
Response: We appreciate the commenters' input. We remind readers that our goal in this rulemaking cycle is to establish the category of SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests and the general payment mechanism for those services under the OPPS, noting that payment alignment is a priority for these technologies. Given the interim nature of the policy, we will take the definitional concerns raised by the commenters, including incorporating additional specificity regarding differences in SaMS service for purposes of Medicare payment, into consideration for future rulemaking. We welcome public engagement from interested parties on these issues, including whether there are services that should be designated as SaMS in the future.
Comment: Some commenters, particularly large laboratory associations, disagreed with the premise underlying our proposal, explaining that the diagnostic testing process as a whole, not the physical location where the final computational step occurs, is what defines a clinical diagnostic laboratory test. These commenters did not agree that the absence of a new wet lab step converts a patient-specific computational analysis of laboratory-derived data into something other than laboratory testing and argued that treating the final analytical step as severable from the laboratory service that produced the underlying data misconstrues how these tests are developed, validated, and clinically interpreted. Relatedly, these commenters requested that CMS confirm in the final rule that a test including a laboratory assay measuring an analyte from the specimen remains a CDLT paid under the CLFS, and that specimen preparation, staining, and digitization are not the “prior laboratory test” on which SaMS designation depends.
Response: We disagree with these commenters that the location of the final analytical step is immaterial to the payment classification of these services. While we recognize that the underlying specimen collection, sequencing, or other data-generating steps may require laboratory services, the algorithmic analysis at issue here is a separate step that is performed on data that has already been generated, and may not necessarily require access to the specimen or laboratory equipment. The fact that a service has historically been billed and paid as a single, integrated CDLT on the CLFS does not mean that each component of that service must continue to be paid as such, particularly where the analytical component is distinguishable from the data-generating component as provided by the HCPCS code descriptor, both in the resources required to perform it and in the manner in which its costs are incurred. Accordingly, we are finalizing our proposal to treat the algorithmic analysis as an “other diagnostic test” distinct from the underlying laboratory test for purposes of OPPS payment. We will take the definitional concerns ( printed page 70631) regarding SaMS into consideration for future rulemaking.
Comment: Several commenters urged CMS to coordinate this policy with the pending CLIA RFI issued by CMS and the CDC on July 16, 2026, regarding the appropriate level of CLIA oversight of “dry lab” facilities that perform computational analyses without a traditional wet-lab component, so that the two efforts do not produce conflicting outcomes.[175] Commenters noted that CMS and the CDC are actively considering, through that RFI, whether CLIA certification is required to furnish these types of services, and argued that it is premature for CMS to conclude in this rule that such services are not “laboratory” services for payment purposes before that RFI is complete. Commenters requested that CMS defer any changes to this OPPS payment policy pending the outcome of the CLIA RFI, given the potential for the policies under consideration there to directly conflict with the proposal at issue here. One commenter separately requested that CMS clarify that CLIA's scope includes facilities that produce and examine information obtained through analysis of materials derived from the human body.
Response: We appreciate these comments. We plan to coordinate and collaborate across the relevant agencies to ensure oversight and payment policies are consistent.
Comment: Commenters requested that CMS confirm it does not intend, in addressing the Medicare billing of SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests, to change the regulatory structure under which laboratories and the tests they provide are governed. Commenters noted that the proposal could be read to create ambiguity on this point and requested that CMS include the following clarifying statement in the final rule: that algorithmic interpretation of specimen-derived pathology data, performed within or under arrangement with a CLIA-certified laboratory, remains subject to CLIA.
Response: This policy does not seek to make changes to the requirements governing CLIA-certified laboratories. We consider these algorithmic analyses as “other diagnostic tests” that are performed on an underlying laboratory test. This policy seeks to provide consistency in paying for all SaMS algorithmic analyses under new technology APCs in the OPPS. We will take the regulatory concerns raised by commenters, including incorporating additional specificity regarding SaMS services and CLIA, into consideration for future rulemaking. We welcome public engagement from interested parties on these issues.
Comment: We received comments regarding the specific list of HCPCS codes we proposed to designate as SaMS laboratory analyses. Commenters generally agreed that the following CPT codes describe algorithmic analyses and may be designated as SaMS laboratory analyses:
0510U—Oncology (pancreatic cancer), augmentative algorithmic analysis of 16 genes from previously sequenced rna whole transcriptome data, reported as probability of predicted molecular subtype
0512U—Oncology (prostate), augmentative algorithmic analysis of digitized whole-slide imaging of histologic features for microsatellite instability (msi) status, formalin-fixed paraffin embedded (ffpe) tissue, reported as increased or decreased probability of msi-high (msi-h)
0513U—Oncology (prostate), augmentative algorithmic analysis of digitized whole-slide imaging of histologic features for microsatellite instability (msi) and homologous recombination deficiency (hrd) status, formalin fixed paraffin-embedded (ffpe) tissue, reported as increased or decreased probability of each biomarker
0418U—Oncology (breast), augmentative algorithmic analysis of digitized whole slide imaging of 8 histologic and immunohistochemical features, reported as a recurrence score
0376U—Oncology (prostate cancer), image analysis of at least 128 histologic features and clinical factors, prognostic algorithm determining the risk of distant metastases, and prostate cancer-specific mortality, includes predictive algorithm to androgen deprivation-therapy response, if appropriate
Response: We thank the commenters for their support. We are finalizing our proposals to assign CPT codes 0510U, 0512U, 0513U, 0418U, and 0376U to new technology APCs for payment under the OPPS as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. Please refer to Table 85 for the list of services we are finalizing as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests.
Comment: We received a comment noting that CPT codes 81417 and 81427 both describe post-sequencing data analysis but were not included in the proposed list of CPT codes to designate as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests for purposes of payment under the OPPS.
We also received a comment noting that CPT codes 81417 ( Exome (e.g., unexplained constitutional or heritable disorder or syndrome); re-evaluation of previously obtained exome sequence (e.g., updated knowledge or unrelated condition/syndrome) and 81427 ( Genome (e.g., unexplained constitutional or heritable disorder or syndrome); re-evaluation of previously obtained genome sequence (e.g., updated knowledge or unrelated condition/syndrome) ) both describe post-sequencing data analysis but were not included in the proposed list of CPT codes to designate as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests for purposes of payment under the OPPS.
Response: We thank the commenter for bringing these codes to our attention. We agree that CPT codes 81417 and 81427 codes should be designated as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests for purposes of payment under the OPPS because they provide a secondary or subsequent stand-alone algorithmic analysis of a previously obtained exome or genome sequence. Therefore, for CY 2027, we are finalizing assigning CPT code 81417 to APC 1505 (New Technology—Level 5 ($301-$400)) and 81427 to APC 1522 (New Technology—Level 22 ($2,001-$2,500)).
Comment: Some commenters asserted that certain codes that we proposed to designate as SaMS analyses performed on tests performed on laboratory tests for payment under the OPPS should not be finalized as proposed because they possess, or may possess, wet lab components. Per the commenters, the following CPT codes have wet lab components:
0511U—Oncology (solid tumor), tumor cell culture in 3d microenvironment, 36 or more drug panel, reported as tumor-response prediction for each drug
81416—Exome (e.g., unexplained constitutional or heritable disorder or syndrome); sequence analysis, each comparator exome (e.g., parents, siblings) (list separately in addition to code for primary procedure)
Similarly, a commenter opposed finalizing CPT code 0414U ( Oncology (lung), augmentative algorithmic analysis of digitized whole slide imaging for 8 genes (alk, braf, egfr, erbb2, met, ntrk1-3, ret, ros1), and kras g12c and pd-l1, if performed, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (ffpe) tissue, reported as positive or negative for each biomarker) as a SaMS analysis ( printed page 70632) performed on a laboratory test for payment under the OPPS because the service includes a wet lab component if performed, as designated in the descriptor. A commenter opposed similarly designating CPT code 0220U ( Oncology (breast cancer), image analysis with artificial intelligence assessment of 12 histologic and immunohistochemical features, reported as a recurrence score) as a SaMS analysis performed on a laboratory test because the code is ambiguous on whether it includes wet lab steps. One commenter pointed out that CPT code 0208U ( Oncology (medullary thyroid carcinoma), mrna, gene expression analysis of 108 genes, utilizing fine needle aspirate, algorithm reported as positive or negative for medullary thyroid carcinoma) was deleted effective January 1, 2022, and therefore, should not be included on the final list for payment under the OPPS.
Response: We agree with commenters that CPT codes 0511U and 81416 both involve wet lab analyses as outlined in each CPT descriptor, and therefore, should not be assigned to new technology APCs for payment under the OPPS. Since the code descriptors integrate both the wet lab and secondary algorithmic analyses, rather than only the computer-based secondary analyses component, we agree to not designate CPT codes 0511U and 81416 as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. These HCPCS codes would continue to be paid under the CLFS.
However, we do not agree with commenters that CPT code 0414U should be paid under the CLFS, as the descriptor characterizes the service as an augmentative algorithmic analysis. Commenters pointed out that the descriptor allows for additional analysis “if performed,” if, for example, a slide needs to be redone for the purpose of the analysis. However, our understanding is that the “if performed” language does not indicate that the algorithmic analysis is optional, but instead refers to the optional analysis of additional biomarkers. Therefore, we are finalizing assignment of CPT code 0414U to a new technology APC for payment under the OPPS as proposed.
Regarding CPT code 0220U, we similarly disagree with the commenters that the code descriptor is ambiguous on whether a wet lab component is included. The descriptor cites “image analysis with artificial intelligence,” which we believe is similar to other SaMS laboratory analyses of existing images or slides.
Finally, we appreciate the comment noting that CPT code 0208U was deleted and agree that it should not be included on the final list for payment under the OPPS.
Comment: We received comments regarding the proposed APC assignments for the services we proposed to designate as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. Some commenters supported crosswalking codes from the CLFS to new technology APCs as proposed, maintaining CY 2026 CLFS payment rates. Some commenters disagreed with the proposed new technology APC assignment for certain HCPCS codes. For example, one commenter requested that we reassign CPT codes 1063T (Oncology (bladder), augmentative algorithmic analysis of histomorphologic features in digitized slides from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) bladder cancer tissue (high-grade, non-muscle invasive), with clinicopathologic variables entered by the qualified health care professional; algorithm-derived parameters reported as prognostic of recurrence and progression, including hematoxylin and eosin staining of tissue sections, and digitization of glass microscope slides, when performed) and 1064T (Oncology (bladder), augmentative algorithmic analysis of histomorphologic features in digitized slides from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) bladder cancer tissue (high-grade, non-muscle invasive), with clinicopathologic variables entered by the qualified health care professional; algorithm-derived parameters reported as predictive of response to Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) therapy, including hematoxylin and eosin staining of tissue sections, and digitization of glass microscope slides, when performed) to APC 1509 (New Technology—Level 9 ($701-$800)) rather than APC 1542 (New Technology—Level 5 ($301-$400)) based on resource costs and similarities to other services we proposed to assign to APC 1509. Commenters also requested that CMS assign substantively comparable specimen-based algorithmic analyses to consistent new technology APC bands, state the basis on which band assignments are made, and establish a mechanism for correcting assignments that are inconsistent with those made for comparable services.
Response: We thank the commenters for their input. We agree with commenters that CPT codes 1063T and 1064T are similar to CPT code 1097T, for which we proposed, and are finalizing, assignment to APC 1509. Therefore, we are finalizing assigning CPT codes 1063T and 1064T to APC 1509 (New Technology—Level 9 ($701-$800)) based on public comments received. Regarding the process for assigning and correcting assignments for comparable SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests to new technology APCs, we remind the commenters that the notice-and-comment rulemaking is an available and appropriate process for requesting initial payment assignments and subsequent payment changes.
Comment: Commenters supported CMS's proposal to base new technology APC payment for these codes on existing CLFS payment rates, using the latest available CLFS data to crosswalk codes to new technology APCs at rates that closely approximate current CLFS payment levels.
Response: We thank the commenters for their support. We agree that CY 2026 CLFS rates for algorithmic analyses, which were the latest available CLFS rates at the time that the proposed rule was drafted, should be maintained with the implementation of this interim policy. We believe it is appropriate to use the current CLFS payment rates for CY 2026, as proposed, to align with the payment policy for SaMS described in the prior section which similarly finalized the proposed payment rates.
Comment: Commenters requested that CMS confirm that superintelligence enabled diagnostic analyses performed in CLIA-certified independent laboratories after the hospital encounter are eligible for separate payment under the OPPS framework. Commenters further requested that CMS permit laboratories to bill Medicare for these services when developed as laboratory-developed tests, noting that if such tests are not billable by laboratories under the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule, laboratories would effectively be prohibited from directly billing and receiving payment for services they perform.
Response: As we stated in the proposed rule, the services that we designate as SaMS, specifically SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests, will be assigned to new technology APCs and a status indicator of `O1' to indicate that these services are SaMS for payment purposes and paid for under the OPPS. We refer readers to the CY 2027 PFS final rule for discussion on how SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests will be paid under PFS.
Comment: A commenter requested that CMS confirm the applicable date of service for algorithm-only laboratory analyses, noting that if such services are classified as “other diagnostic tests” rather than clinical diagnostic laboratory tests, the laboratory date of service policy would not apply.
Response: We confirm that because we are classifying SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests as “other diagnostic tests” under section ( printed page 70633) 1861(s)(3) of the Act, they would not be subject to the date of service policy as outlined in 42 CFR 414.510.
Comment: Regarding CMS's proposed definition of status indicator “O1,” a commenter requested that CMS avoid applying a multiple-procedure payment reduction to algorithm-only analyses, explaining that such services do not meet the criteria typically underlying that reduction because each algorithm is typically a distinct, independently developed and validated analytic service answering a distinct clinical question.
Response: We agree. We refer readers to the earlier discussion in this section regarding the payment specifications for status indicator “O1,” which we are finalizing to treat as “S” (Procedure or Service, Not Discounted When Multiple) to allow for separate payment without multiple procedure discounting.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal for CY 2027 to reassign certain HCPCS codes describing SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests that are currently paid under the CLFS to new technology APC assignments under the OPPS. However, we are finalizing the proposed code list with certain modifications, based on public comments received. In total, for CY 2027, we are finalizing to assign 14 SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests to new technology APCs. Additionally, we are finalizing our proposal for CY 2027 and subsequent years, to assign any new SaMS analyses performed on laboratory test codes to new technology APCs for payment under the OPPS. We note that this is an interim first step to address the concerns regarding the proliferation of SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. We intend to continue to engage with the laboratory community on these finalized changes, and acknowledge the definitional concerns regarding SaMS services and the applicable payment and regulatory frameworks. We will consider expanding and further clarifying the scope of the policy through future rulemaking.
Refer to Table 85 for the final new technology APC and status indicator assignments for SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests for CY 2027. The final CY 2027 payment rates can be found in Addendum B to this final rule with comment period via the internet on the CMS website. In addition, we refer readers to Addendum D1 to this final rule with comment period for the status indicator meanings for all codes reported under the OPPS. Addendum D1 can also be found via the internet on the CMS website.
3. Summary of CY 2027 SaMS Final Payment Policies
In summary, for CY 2027, we are finalizing the following interim payment policies. First, we are finalizing a terminology change from SaaS to SaMS to more accurately describe algorithm-based software services. Second, we are creating a new status indicator “O1” (Software as a Medical Service, paid under OPPS; separate APC payment) to designate SaMS that are payable under the OPPS. Third, we are finalizing assignment of all SaMS assigned to status indicator “O1” to a new technology APC. For CY 2027, we are maintaining the payment rates consistent for SaMS assigned to status indicator “O1” from CY 2026 OPPS rates. In addition, we are finalizing our proposal to use the term “SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests” to describe stand-alone algorithmic analyses of data generated by a prior laboratory test. Although the services we have designated as SaMS in section X.B.1. of the final rule with comment period are required to have FDA marketing authorization to receive Medicare payment, “SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests do not currently require FDA marketing authorization in order to receive payment under OPPS. While these secondary analyses are currently paid for under the CLFS as “diagnostic laboratory tests” under section 1861(s)(3), (16), and (17) of the Act, for CY 2027, we are finalizing our position that these services are “other diagnostic tests” and, therefore, will be paid under OPPS under section 1861(s)(3) of the Act. Specifically, we are finalizing payment for 14 SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests from the CLFS to the OPPS by assigning the codes to new technology APCs that align with current CY 2026 CLFS payment rates.
C. Adjustment for Cost-of-Living in Alaska and Hawaii
We have heard from a variety of interested parties about the particularly difficult cost environment facing hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii. These challenges stem from the unique circumstances of those geographies, including dependency on outside goods and components, remote locations and transportation challenges, and other factors inherent to providing healthcare in these non-contiguous States.
A review of the available cost report data used in OPPS ratesetting highlights these issues. We stated in the proposed rule that we observed a number of hospitals in Alaska and Hawaii with payment-to-cost ratios (PCRs) that range from 0.6 to 0.7, significantly below the average PCR for OPPS hospitals of 0.89 used as an initial target for the cancer hospital adjustment discussed in section II.F. of the proposed rule. In addition, the overall ancillary cost-to-charge ratios for several hospitals located in these States are higher than average, indicating that there are higher costs relative to what those hospitals charge for the outpatient services they provide compared to other OPPS hospitals.
Under the IPPS, section 1886(d)(5)(H) of the Act provides discretionary authority to the Secretary to make adjustments as the Secretary deems appropriate to take into account the unique circumstances of hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii. To account for higher non-labor-related costs for these two States in the IPPS, we apply an adjustment factor to the nonlabor-related portion of the standardized amount for hospitals in Alaska and Hawaii. For FY 2011 and in prior fiscal years, we used the most recent cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) factors obtained from the U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) website at https://www.opm.gov/​policy-data-oversight/​pay-leave/​pay-systems/​nonforeign-areas/​#url=​COLA-Rates to update this nonlabor portion.
In the FY 2013 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule, we established a methodology to update the COLA factors for Alaska and Hawaii that were published by the U.S. OPM every 4 years (coinciding with the update to the labor-related share of the IPPS market basket), beginning in FY 2014. We refer readers to the FY 2013 IPPS/LTCH PPS proposed and final rules for additional background and a detailed description of this methodology (77 FR 28145 through 28146 and 77 FR 53700 through 53701, respectively). In the FY 2022 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule (86 FR 45546 through 45547), we updated the COLA factors published by OPM for 2009 (as these are the last COLA factors OPM published prior to transitioning from COLAs to locality pay) using the methodology that we finalized in the FY 2013 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule and Consumer Price Indices (CPIs) data through 2020. Based on the policy finalized in the FY 2013 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule, we utilized these COLA factors for FYs 2022 through 2025 to adjust the nonlabor-related portion of the standardized amount for hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii.
As we discussed in the proposed rule, in general, under the IPPS methodology, we updated the 2009 OPM COLA factors by a comparison of the growth in the CPIs for the areas of Urban Alaska and Urban Hawaii, relative to the growth in the CPI for the average U.S. city as published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). We used the comparison of the growth in the overall CPI relative to the growth in the CPI for those areas to update the COLA factors for all areas in Alaska and Hawaii, respectively, because BLS publishes CPI data for only Urban Alaska and Urban Hawaii. Using the respective CPI commodities index and CPI services index, and using the approximate commodities/services shares obtained from the IPPS market basket, we created reweighted CPIs for each of the respective areas to reflect the underlying composition of the IPPS market basket nonlabor-related share. Lastly, we exercised our discretionary authority to adjust payments to hospitals in Alaska and Hawaii by including the statutorily mandated cap of 25 percent that was applied when determining OPM's COLA factors. (For additional information, refer to the FY 2022 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule (86 FR 45546 through 45547).
As discussed in the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS proposed rule, effective for FY 2027, we proposed to adjust non-labor related costs for hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii, using the Overseas Cost-of-Living Allowance (OCOLA) data published by the Department of Defense (DOD). Starting with the FY 2027 payment year, we also proposed to no longer cap the IPPS COLA factors at 25 percent. We refer readers to the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS proposed rule for further discussion of the proposed changes to the methodology for calculating the IPPS COLA factors for FY 2027 (91 FR 19813 through 19814).
As discussed in the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule, after consideration of public comments, we finalized our proposed methodology to use the DOD OCOLAs to determine the COLA factors, to no longer cap these OCOLA-based COLA factors at 25 percent, and to continue to update the COLA factors in conjunction with the labor-related share of the IPPS market basket. However, given concerns raised by commenters, in particular that the OCOLA data may not reflect some of the high costs directly affecting Hawaii, for any locality area where the COLA factors would decrease using the DOD OCOLA data, we stated that we will maintain the COLA factors that were in place for FY 2022 through FY 2026. Therefore, we finalized the use of the DOD OCOLAs to determine the COLAs for each of the designated OPM areas in Alaska and for the designated OPM areas for County of Hawaii and County of Kauai and to no longer cap these ( printed page 70637) OCOLA-based COLA factors at 25 percent. For the areas of City and County of Honolulu and County of Maui and County of Kalawao, given that the DOD OCOLA data would result in a decrease in the COLA factor, we finalized to maintain the current COLA factors of 1.25. Table H-01 of the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule lists the finalized IPPS COLA factors for FY 2027 for the OPM designated areas of Alaska and Hawaii (91 FR 50389).
While higher labor-related costs for these two States are taken into account under the OPPS through the adoption of the IPPS hospital wage index and associated wage index policies, the nonlabor portion of OPPS payment is not currently adjusted to address higher nonlabor costs in these States as is addressed in the IPPS through the COLA policy. We have historically adopted the IPPS wage index and wage index policies under the OPPS, most recently in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (90 FR 53494 through 53498). As discussed in section II.C of the proposed rule, we proposed to continue to adopt the IPPS wage index and wage index policies under the CY 2027 OPPS and also continue to believe that using the IPPS wage index as the source of an adjustment factor for the OPPS is reasonable and logical, given the inseparable, subordinate status of the HOPD within the hospital overall. We think this same logic would apply to adopting the IPPS COLA policy for hospital outpatient services in Alaska and Hawaii, as additional nonlabor costs that apply to hospital inpatient services provided in these States likely also apply to hospital outpatient services in these States. Further, not addressing the discrepancy between the IPPS and OPPS adjustment to account for nonlabor related costs would potentially continue a disincentive to provide services in the hospital outpatient setting due to the adjustment only applying to inpatient services.
Based on our review of the costs of providing outpatient services in these States and our general practice of applying consistent policies across the inpatient and outpatient hospital settings where possible, we proposed to use the equitable adjustment authority provided by section 1833(t)(2)(E) of the Act to propose to apply the IPPS COLA factors to the nonlabor share of OPPS payment amounts for hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii for CY 2027 and future years. We note that for OPPS payments for which there is no wage adjustable portion, we proposed to apply the COLA to the full OPPS payment, as would be the case for status indicator assignments of “G,” “H,” “K,” “R,” and “U”.
As noted earlier in this section, in the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS proposed rule we proposed several changes to the current COLA methodology including using the OCOLA data published by the DOD for the FY 2027 factors as well as to remove the cap of 25 percent (91 FR 19813 through 19814). Consistent with our historical practice of aligning OPPS payment methodologies with those of the IPPS where appropriate, we proposed to adopt the IPPS COLA factors as finalized in the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule as the CY 2027 OPPS COLA factors for hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii. As previously discussed in this section, Table H-01 of the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule lists the IPPS COLA factors finalized for FY 2027 for the OPM designated areas of Alaska and Hawaii (91 FR 50389).
Under the OPPS, section 1833(t)(2)(E) of the Act grants the Secretary the authority to establish equitable adjustments as necessary, and we proposed to use that authority to establish a COLA for outpatient hospital services provided in Alaska and Hawaii that mirrors the COLA provided for inpatient hospital services provided in these States. Associated with this proposed policy, we also proposed to add conforming regulation text changes by adding subsection (l) to § 419.43. This new subsection describes the cost-of-living adjustment to the nonlabor portion of the OPPS payment amounts for hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii. Finally, we noted that under our authority at section 1833(t)(2)(E) of the Act this adjustment would be budget neutral, and stated that the associated budget neutrality adjustment is discussed in section II.B. of the proposed rule.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Several commenters supported the proposal to establish a COLA for hospital outpatient services furnished in Alaska and Hawaii. Several commenters requested that CMS finalize the proposal without delay and align the outpatient adjustment with the final IPPS COLA factors.
Response: We thank the commenters for their support.
Comment: One commenter stated that the proposed rule did not clearly identify the full set of payable services to which the COLA applies. The comment asked whether the adjustment is limited to status indicators G, H, K, R, and U or also applies to H1, J1, J2, K1, P, S, T, V, and other payable indicators.
Response: We appreciate the request for clarification. For OPPS payments that include a wage-adjustable portion, the COLA would apply to the nonlabor-related portion of the payment after the applicable wage adjustment is determined. This would apply to OPPS payments associated with final status indicators “J1,” “J2,” “O1,” “P,” “S,” “T,” and “V.”
For OPPS payments for which there is no wage-adjustable portion, including payments for services assigned status indicators “G,” “H,” “H1,” “K,” “K1,” “R,” “S1,” and “U,” the COLA would apply to the full OPPS payment amount. We are clarifying this distinction because these payments do not contain a separately identified labor-related portion to which the hospital wage index would otherwise apply.
Comment: A commenter requested that CMS implement the OPPS COLA in a manner that avoids unintended reductions for hospitals affected by the revised FY 2027 IPPS methodology. The commenter noted that, in the FY 2027 IPPS final rule, CMS maintained the existing payment levels for some of the areas in Hawaii and asked that CMS do the same the OPPS.
Response: In the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule (91 FR 50389), we are maintaining the COLA factors that were in place for FY 2022 through FY 2026 for City and County of Honolulu, County of Maui, and County of Kalawao for FY 2027. Under our proposal, the same IPPS COLA factors as finalized in the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule would be adopted as the CY 2027 OPPS COLA factors for hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii. We refer readers to Table H-01 of the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule, which lists the IPPS COLA factors finalized for FY 2027 for the OPM designated areas of Alaska and Hawaii (91 FR 50389). Comment: A commenter supported the proposed COLA but encouraged CMS to continue evaluating alternative data sources that may more accurately reflect healthcare-specific costs in Alaska and Hawaii. The commenter suggested that CMS consider state-level cost-of-living measures, healthcare-specific inflation indexes, construction costs, transportation costs, utility costs, and supply-chain measures.
Response: We appreciate the commenter's recommendations concerning potential alternative data sources. For CY 2027, we believe it is appropriate to use the COLA factors finalized under the FY 2027 IPPS because doing so provides consistency ( printed page 70638) between the inpatient and outpatient hospital payment systems.
We refer readers to the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule, where we invited feedback and suggestions regarding any additional data sources that could be used to develop the COLA factors (91 FR 50388).
Comment: One commenter believed that the COLA would establish an asymmetry in which hospitals receiving low wages would contribute to financing the COLA through OPPS budget neutrality without receiving comparable recognition for their geographic circumstances. The commenter asked CMS to explain this difference or provide more substantial relief through modifying budget neutrality for the OPPS wage-index transitional exception to specifically apply to hospitals above the 75th percentile of wage indexes.
Response: We appreciate the commenter's concerns but do not agree that the COLA and wage-index policies create the asserted asymmetry. The hospital wage index and COLA apply to address different cost categories and payment portions. The wage index is used to adjust the portion of the OPPS payment that is labor-related to account for different geographic levels of hospital wage costs. The COLA is designed to adjust the portion of payments not related to labor costs, so as to account for the distinct nonlabor costs of furnishing services in Alaska and Hawaii.
The presence of a nonlabor COLA for Alaska and Hawaii thus does not indicate that the wage-index methodology is failing to recognize geographic variation in labor costs elsewhere. Hospitals outside Alaska and Hawaii continue to receive wage index and other geographic adjustments applicable to them under both the IPPS and OPPS.
Section 1833(t)(2)(E) of the Act mandates that equitable adjustments are made in a budget-neutral manner, requiring that associated changes do not affect estimated aggregate OPPS expenditures. We do not believe that it is appropriate to budget neutralize specifically to hospitals with wage indexes above the 75th percentile. Developing wage index budget neutrality in this manner would result in different wage indexes between the IPPS and OPPS, we believe that it is important to maintain alignment of the IPPS and OPPS wage indexes,
We therefore do not believe that establishing the COLA in the OPPS necessitates implementation of an additional wage index adjustment or altering the calculation of budget neutrality with regards to the wage index and its associated adjustments. For a detailed discussion of the wage index, please see section II.C. of this final rule with comment period.
Comment: Commenters agreed that circumstances in Alaska and Hawaii lead to higher non-labor costs, but stated that rural communities in other States also have geographic barriers to access care, shortages of health care workers, long travelling distances, transportation limitations, and other access limitations. One commenter stated, in general, that CMS allow for regional variation for cost-of-living.
Response: The OPPS addresses certain geographic differences through other payment policies, including application of the hospital wage index to the labor-related portion of the OPPS payment, the rural sole community hospital adjustment, geographic reclassification, and the out-migration adjustment. The OPPS COLA policy serves a narrower purpose. It recognizes the unique non-labor costs experienced by hospitals in the two non-contiguous states, Alaksa and Hawaii, and aligns the OPPS treatment of those costs with the longstanding IPPS policy.
After consideration of the public comments and for the reasons discussed, we are finalizing our proposal to apply the finalized IPPS COLA factors to the non-labor portion of OPPS payment for hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii for CY 2027 and future years. We are also finalizing the proposed conforming regulation text changes at 42 CFR 419.43(l) and the associated budget neutrality adjustment as discussed in section II.B. of this final rule with comment period.

XII. MedPAC Recommendations
The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC) was established under section 1805 of the Act in large part to advise the U.S. Congress on issues affecting the Medicare program. As required under the statute, MedPAC submits reports to Congress no later than March and June of each year that present its Medicare payment policy recommendations. The March report typically provides discussion of Medicare payment policy across different payment systems and the June report typically discusses selected Medicare issues. We are including this section to make interested parties aware of certain MedPAC recommendations for the OPPS and ASC payment systems as discussed in its March 2026 report.
Comments received from MedPAC for other OPPS or ASC payment system policies are discussed in the applicable sections of this final rule with comment period.
A. OPPS Payment Rates Update
The March 2026 MedPAC “Report to the Congress: Medicare Payment Policy”, recommended that the Congress update Medicare OPPS payment rates by the amount specified in current law. We refer readers to the March 2026 report for a complete discussion of this recommendation.[177] We appreciate MedPAC's recommendation and, as discussed further in section II.B. of this final rule with comment period, we are finalizing our proposal to increase the OPPS payment rates by the amount specified in current law.
B. Medicare Safety Net Index
In the March 2026 MedPAC “Report to the Congress: Medicare Payment Policy”, MedPAC stated that their recommended update to IPPS and OPPS payment rates under current law may not be sufficient to ensure the financial viability of some Medicare safety-net hospitals with a poor payer mix. MedPAC recommended that Congress redistribute the current Medicare safety-net payments (disproportionate share hospital and uncompensated care payments) using the MedPAC-developed Medicare Safety-Net Index (MSNI) for hospitals. In addition, MedPAC recommended adding $1 billion to this MSNI pool of funds to help maintain the financial viability of Medicare safety-net hospitals and recommended to the Congress transitional approaches for an MSNI policy. The FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH final rule with comment period (91 FR 49570) provides additional information regarding statutory requirements for disproportionate share hospital and uncompensated care payments. We look forward to working with Congress on these matters.

B. ASC Treatment of New and Revised Codes
1. Background on Process for New and Revised HCPCS Codes
We update the lists and payment rates for covered surgical procedures and covered ancillary services in ASCs in conjunction with the annual proposed and final rulemaking process to update the OPPS and the ASC payment systems (§ 416.173; 72 FR 42535). We base ASC payment and policies for most covered surgical procedures, drugs, biologicals, and certain other covered ancillary services on the OPPS payment policies, and we use quarterly change requests (CRs) to update services paid for under the OPPS. We also provide quarterly update CRs for ASC covered surgical procedures and covered ancillary services throughout the year (January, April, July, and October). We release new and revised Level II HCPCS codes and recognize the release of new and revised CPT codes by the American Medical Association (AMA) and make these codes effective (that is, the codes are recognized on Medicare claims) via these ASC quarterly update CRs. We recognize the release of new and revised Category III CPT codes in the July and January CRs. We note however, that in early August of this year, the AMA updated their `release and effective date' schedule for Category III CPT codes. The Category III CPT codes will no longer be released only twice a year. Category III CPT codes will be released April 1 with an effective date of July 1, July 1 with an effective date of October 1, and October 1 with an effective date of January 1.[178] These codes will be recognized in the July, October, and January CRs. These updates implement newly created and revised Level II HCPCS and Category III CPT codes for ASC payments and update the payment rates for separately paid drugs and biologicals based on the most recently submitted ASP data. New and revised Category I CPT codes, except vaccine codes, are released only once a year, and are implemented only through the January quarterly CR update. New and revised Category I CPT vaccine codes are released twice a year and are implemented through the January and July quarterly CR updates. We refer ( printed page 70641) readers to Table 41 in the CY 2012 OPPS/ASC proposed rule for an example of how this process is used to update HCPCS and CPT codes, which we finalized in the CY 2012 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (76 FR 42291; 76 FR 74380 through 74384).
In our annual updates to the ASC list of covered surgical procedures and covered ancillary services, we undertake a review of excluded surgical procedures, new codes, and codes with revised descriptors, to identify any that we believe meet the criteria for designation as ASC covered surgical procedures or covered ancillary services. Updating the lists of ASC covered surgical procedures and covered ancillary services, as well as their payment rates, in association with the annual OPPS rulemaking cycle, is particularly important because the OPPS relative payment weights and, in some cases, payment rates, are used as the basis for the payment of many covered surgical procedures and covered ancillary services under the revised ASC payment system. This joint update process ensures that the ASC updates occur in a regular, predictable, and timely manner.
Payment for ASC procedures, services, and items are generally based on medical billing codes, specifically, HCPCS codes, that are reported on ASC claims. The HCPCS is divided into two principal subsystems, referred to as Level I and Level II. Level I is comprised of CPT (Current Procedural Terminology) codes, a numeric and alphanumeric coding system maintained by the AMA, and includes Category I, II, and III CPT codes. Level II of the HCPCS, which is maintained by CMS, is a standardized coding system that is used primarily to identify products, supplies, and services not included in the CPT codes. Together, Level I and II HCPCS codes are used to report procedures, services, items, and supplies under the ASC payment system. Specifically, we recognize the following codes on ASC claims:
Category I CPT codes, which describe surgical procedures, diagnostic and therapeutic services, and vaccine codes;
Category III CPT codes, which describe new and emerging technologies, services, and procedures; and
Level II HCPCS codes (also known as alpha-numeric codes), which are used primarily to identify drugs, devices, supplies, temporary procedures, and services not described by CPT codes.
We finalized a policy in the August 2, 2007 ASC final rule (72 FR 42533 through 42535) to evaluate each year all new and revised Category I and Category III CPT codes and Level II HCPCS codes that describe surgical procedures, and to make preliminary determinations during the annual OPPS/ASC rulemaking process regarding whether or not they meet the criteria for payment in the ASC setting as covered surgical procedures and, if so, whether or not they are office-based procedures. In addition, we identify new and revised codes as ASC covered ancillary services based upon the final payment policies of the revised ASC payment system. In prior rulemakings, we refer to this process as recognizing new codes. However, this process has always involved the recognition of new and revised codes. We consider revised codes to be new when they have substantial revision to their code descriptors that necessitate a change in the current ASC payment indicator. To clarify, we refer to these codes as new and revised in this final rule with comment period.
We have separated our discussion later in this section of the preamble based on when the codes are released and whether we proposed to solicit public comments in the proposed rule (and respond to those comments in this CY 2027 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period) or whether we will be soliciting public comments in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (and responding to those comments in the CY 2028 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period).
